Finally, excessive logging at debug level in production inflates costs, so use sampling and configurable levels per component.
How do Linux file permissions work?

Every file and directory in Linux has three sets of permissions: one for the owner, one for the owning group, and one for everyone else. Each set can include read (r), write (w), and execute (x). For regular files, read allows viewing contents, write allows modifying them, and execute allows running them as a program or script. For directories, read allows listing contents, write allows creating, deleting, or renaming entries, and execute allows entering the directory and accessing files within it. You can view permissions with ls -l, which shows a string like -rwxr-x--- where the first character indicates the file type, followed by the owner, group, and other permission triplets. Permissions can also be expressed in octal, where r=4, w=2, and x=1 are summed per set, so rwxr-x--- becomes 750.
How do I change those permissions from the command line?

The chmod command changes permissions. You can use symbolic mode, such as chmod u+x script.sh to add execute for the owner, chmod g-w file.txt to remove write from the group, or chmod o=r file.txt to set others to read only. Octal mode sets all bits at once, so chmod 644 file.txt gives the owner read and write, and group and others read only. The -R flag applies changes recursively to a directory and its contents. Only the file owner or root can change a file's permissions. To change ownership, use chown, for example chown alice:developers project.txt, which sets the owner to alice and the group to developers. Use sudo when you lack the required privileges.
What do the setuid, setgid, and sticky bits do?

These are special permission bits that sit above the standard triplets. The setuid bit (4000) on an executable makes it run with the privileges of the file owner rather than the user who launched it; the passwd command uses this so ordinary users can update the protected shadow file. The setgid bit (2000) on an executable works similarly for groups, while on a directory it causes new files to inherit the directory's group. The sticky bit (1000) on a directory, as seen on /tmp, allows users to delete only files they own, even if the directory is world-writable. In ls -l output these appear as s or t in the execute position, such as -rwsr-xr-x, or as capital S or T when execute is not set. Set them with chmod, for example chmod 1777 /shared or chmod u+s program.
What does SIGTERM do compared to SIGKILL on Linux?

SIGTERM (signal 15) asks a process to terminate gracefully. The process can catch the signal, run cleanup code such as flushing buffers, closing files, or removing temporary files, and then exit. It can also ignore the signal or block it entirely. SIGKILL (signal 9) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored by the process. The kernel terminates the process immediately, and the process gets no chance to clean up. Because of this, SIGKILL should be a last resort. The usual practice is to send SIGTERM first, wait a short period, and only use SIGKILL if the process has not exited. Note that SIGKILL can leave behind resources such as shared memory segments or lock files that the program would normally release on shutdown.
How do I send one of these signals to a process if I only know its name?

You can use pkill or killall. For example, pkill -TERM nginx sends SIGTERM to every process whose name matches nginx. The -f flag matches against the full command line instead of just the process name, which helps when several programs share a name. To target a specific process, use kill with its PID, such as kill -TERM 4242. To find the PID first, run pgrep -l nginx, which lists matching PIDs with their names. Before sending a signal to a pattern match, it is wise to run pgrep with the same pattern to confirm exactly which processes will be affected, since a loose pattern can match unintended processes.
What happens if a process receives SIGTERM but is stuck in an uninterruptible sleep?

A process in uninterruptible sleep, shown with state D in ps or top, is usually waiting on a kernel operation such as disk I/O or an NFS request. In this state the process does not act on signals until the kernel operation completes. The SIGTERM is queued as pending, so the process will not exit on its own, and SIGKILL also remains pending. Sending more signals will not help. The process will typically terminate once the blocking operation returns, which may take a long time if the storage or network is failing. If the underlying resource is permanently unavailable, the process may remain in state D until the system is rebooted. You can inspect what the kernel is waiting on by reading /proc/PID/stack or /proc/PID/wchan, which can help diagnose the underlying hardware or filesystem problem.
Is there a way to see which signals a process is currently blocking or ignoring?

Yes, the /proc/PID/status file lists signal masks in hexadecimal. The SigPnd field shows pending signals for the thread, ShdPnd shows pending signals for the whole process, SigBlk shows blocked signals, SigIgn shows ignored signals, and SigCgt shows signals with a installed handler. Each field is a bitmask where bit N-1 corresponds to signal N. To decode a mask, you can use the command grep Sig /proc/PID/status, then convert the hex value with a tool such as capsh --decode or a short shell calculation. Alternatively, the pending-signal fields are straightforward to interpret: if bit 14 is set in SigBlk, then signal 15, SIGTERM, is blocked. This information is useful when a program refuses to stop, because it reveals whether the process is ignoring the signal or has a handler that prevents termination.
How does SSH key-based authentication work at a high level?

SSH key-based authentication uses asymmetric cryptography. A key pair is generated, consisting of a private key and a public key. The public key is copied to the remote server and placed in the file ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for the target account. The private key stays on the client and is never transmitted. When connecting, the server sends a challenge, and the client proves possession of the private key by signing data with it. The server verifies the signature using the stored public key. If the signature is valid, access is granted without a password. Because the private key is never sent over the network, the scheme resists password guessing and eavesdropping, though the private key itself must be protected, often with a passphrase.
What's the difference between Ed25519 and RSA keys, and which is generally recommended today?

Ed25519 is an elliptic-curve signature scheme based on Curve25519. It offers strong security with short keys, typically 256 bits, which produce compact public keys and fast signing and verification. RSA is an older scheme based on factoring large integers, and secure RSA keys generally need at least 2048 bits, with 3072 or 4096 bits common for longer-lived keys. RSA keys are larger and slower to generate at high sizes. Ed25519 is generally recommended today for new keys because it is secure, fast, and has a simpler implementation with fewer parameter choices. RSA remains useful for compatibility with older systems or software that does not support Ed25519. You can generate an Ed25519 key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519.
How should I manage a passphrase so I don't have to type it every time I connect?

An SSH agent holds decrypted private keys in memory so the passphrase is entered only once per session. The ssh-agent program is started, often automatically by the desktop environment, and keys are added with ssh-add, which prompts for the passphrase once. On macOS, ssh-add --apple-use-keychain can store the passphrase in the system keychain so it persists across reboots. Agent forwarding with ssh -A can extend the agent to remote hosts, but it should be used cautiously, since a compromised intermediate host could use the forwarded agent while you are connected. Alternatively, a ProxyJump or ProxyCommand setting allows jumping through a bastion host without forwarding the agent. Keys can also be limited in lifetime with ssh-add -t seconds.
What are good practices for rotating or revoking SSH keys across many servers?

Good practice starts with an inventory: record which public keys are authorized on which accounts and who owns each key. Centralizing authorization helps, for example using a configuration management tool to manage authorized_keys files, or an SSH certificate authority, where servers trust a CA public key and accept user certificates that expire automatically. Certificates avoid distributing individual keys and make revocation simpler, since short lifetimes limit exposure. To rotate a key, generate the new pair, add the new public key everywhere, verify access, and then remove the old entry. To revoke quickly, delete the public key line from every authorized_keys file and, for certificate setups, add the certificate serial to a revocation list such as RevokedKeys. Auditing with periodic scans of authorized_keys files helps catch forgotten or unexpected entries.
What's the difference between git rebase and git merge?

Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they do it differently. git merge creates a new merge commit that has two parents, one from each branch, so the full history of both branches is preserved exactly as it happened. git rebase instead takes the commits unique to your current branch, sets them aside, moves the branch pointer to the tip of the target branch, and then replays those commits one by one on top. The result is a linear history with no merge commit, but the replayed commits get new hashes. Merge is non-destructive and safe for shared branches, while rebase rewrites history, which is why the common guidance is to avoid rebasing commits that others have already pulled.
So when would someone pick rebase over merge in practice?

A common case is keeping a feature branch up to date with main. Running git rebase main on a private feature branch replays your work on the latest main, so when you open a pull request, the diff is clean and the history reads as one straight line. Developers also use interactive rebase, git rebase -i, to squash, reorder, or reword messy local commits before sharing them. Merge tends to be preferred when you want to record that a branch was integrated at a specific point, or when the branch is shared and others have based work on it. Many teams use a mix: rebase local work, then merge into the main branch with a merge commit or a squash merge.
What should I do if a rebase causes conflicts partway through?

Git stops the rebase at the commit that conflicts and marks the conflicting files. You resolve the conflicts in those files, stage them with git add, and then run git rebase --continue to apply the next commit. If the resolution is too complicated, git rebase --abort returns the branch to exactly where it was before you started, which is a safe way to back out. If you would rather skip a single problematic commit entirely, git rebase --skip drops it. Because each commit is replayed separately, you may face the same conflict several times across a long series of commits. Enabling git rerere, which records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically, can reduce this repetition.
How does git bisect work?

git bisect performs a binary search through commit history to find the commit that introduced a bug. You start by marking a known bad commit with git bisect bad, usually the current HEAD, and a known good commit with git bisect good <commit>, such as an older tag or release. Git then checks out a commit roughly halfway between them. You test that revision and report the result with git bisect good or git bisect bad. Each answer eliminates half of the remaining candidates, so a range of 1,000 commits needs only about 10 steps. When the search narrows to a single commit, git prints its identity and the bisect is complete. Running git bisect reset returns your working tree to the branch you started on.
What's the difference between git bisect run and manually testing each step?

git bisect run automates the loop by executing a script at each step. You pass it a command such as git bisect run ./test.sh. Git checks out the midpoint commit, runs the script, and interprets its exit code: 0 means good, 125 means skip the commit because it cannot be built or tested, and any code from 1 to 127 except 125 means bad. The script can be a test suite, a grep for a regression, or a build check. Manual bisection suits cases where the bug needs human judgment, such as a visual glitch or a slow performance feel. Automated runs are faster and reproducible, and they avoid mistakes from tired reviewing, but the script must reliably distinguish good from bad behavior, or the search will converge on the wrong commit.
What should I do if some commits in the range cannot be built?

You can use git bisect skip when you cannot test a commit. Running git bisect skip marks the current revision as untestable, and git picks a different nearby commit to test next. Skipping works well for isolated broken commits, such as a mid-series commit that fails to compile. If many commits are skipped, git may end with a set of candidate commits rather than one, and it reports that the first bad commit lies among them. You can also handle this in automated runs by having the script exit with 125. Another option is to narrow the test itself, for example by making the script tolerant of a missing dependency, so that the build failure does not look like the bug. Once finished, run git bisect reset to restore your original branch.
Can git bisect find a bug that was introduced and then fixed later, or one that only appears intermittently?

For a bug that was introduced and later fixed, bisect still works as long as you define good and bad correctly for the question you are asking. If you want the commit that first introduced the behavior, the bad commit should be one where the bug exists, and the good commit should be one before it appeared, even if the bug is fixed in HEAD. Intermittent bugs are harder because a single test run can give a misleading answer. You can script the test to run several times and fail if any run fails, which catches flaky failures but may mark good commits as bad. Tools like git bisect run combined with a loop, or repeated manual checks at suspicious commits, improve reliability. Recording the result of each step with git bisect log and replaying it with git bisect replay helps you verify the search later.
How does semantic versioning work?

Semantic versioning, often called SemVer, uses a three-part version number in the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, such as 2.4.1. The MAJOR number increases when a release contains incompatible changes to the public API, meaning existing callers may break. The MINOR number increases when functionality is added in a backward-compatible way. The PATCH number increases when backward-compatible bug fixes are made. When a number is incremented, the numbers to its right reset to zero, so going from 2.4.1 to a minor release gives 2.5.0. Pre-release labels such as 1.0.0-beta.1 and build metadata such as 1.0.0+20240101 can be appended, though they are treated differently in precedence rules.
Why do pre-release versions like 1.0.0-alpha sort before 1.0.0?

A pre-release version has lower precedence than the associated normal version. Under the SemVer specification, 1.0.0-alpha comes before 1.0.0 because pre-releases signal that the version is unstable and not yet intended for general use. Identifiers within the pre-release part are compared dot by dot. Numeric identifiers are compared as integers, alphanumeric identifiers are compared lexically in ASCII order, and numeric identifiers always have lower precedence than alphanumeric ones. So alpha.1 comes before alpha.beta, and 1.0.0-alpha.2 comes before 1.0.0-alpha.10 because 2 is less than 10 numerically. Build metadata is ignored when determining precedence.
What's the difference between a caret range and a tilde range when a package uses semver?

Both are version range operators used in dependency managers like npm. A tilde range such as ~1.2.3 allows patch-level updates, so it matches 1.2.x and anything from 1.2.3 up to but not including 1.3.0. A caret range such as ^1.2.3 allows updates that do not change the leftmost non-zero digit, so it matches 1.x.x from 1.2.3 up to but not including 2.0.0. For versions starting with zero, the caret behaves more narrowly: ^0.2.3 matches only 0.2.x, and ^0.0.3 matches only 0.0.3. Caret is the default in npm when saving dependencies, making it more permissive about minor updates than tilde.
What are the main S3 storage classes and how do they differ?

S3 offers several storage classes optimized for different access patterns. S3 Standard is for frequently accessed data and provides millisecond latency with no retrieval fees. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on usage, with no retrieval charges but a small monthly monitoring fee per object. S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are for data accessed less often but needing rapid access when requested; they have lower storage prices but charge a per-GB retrieval fee and a minimum storage duration of 30 days. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Glacier Deep Archive are for archival data, with decreasing storage costs and increasing retrieval times, from milliseconds to up to 12 hours.
What is the difference between Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Deep Archive?

Both are archival classes, but they trade off cost against retrieval speed. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers expedited retrieval in 1 to 5 minutes, standard retrieval in 3 to 5 hours, and bulk retrieval in 5 to 12 hours. It has a minimum storage duration of 90 days. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class in S3, with standard retrieval in 12 hours and bulk retrieval in up to 48 hours. It does not offer expedited retrieval. Its minimum storage duration is 180 days. Deep Archive suits data rarely needed, such as regulatory records kept for many years, while Flexible Retrieval suits archives that may need occasional faster access.
If I wanted to move objects to a cheaper class automatically over time, how would lifecycle rules help?

S3 Lifecycle rules let you define actions that transition objects to another storage class or expire them after a set number of days since creation. A rule can be scoped to an entire bucket, a key prefix, or objects with specific tags. For example, a rule might move objects to Standard-IA after 30 days, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days, and to Deep Archive after 180 days, then delete them after 7 years. Transitions must follow supported paths: you can move objects from Standard to cheaper classes, but you cannot transition back to Standard. Also note that small objects under 128 KB are not transitioned to IA or archive classes by lifecycle rules, and minimum storage duration charges still apply if an object is deleted or moved early.
Does Intelligent-Tiering avoid those minimum storage duration charges, and how does it compare to setting lifecycle rules manually?

Yes, Intelligent-Tiering has no minimum storage duration charge and no retrieval fees, so objects can be accessed or removed at any time without that penalty. Its trade-off is a monthly monitoring and automation charge per object, and objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored for tiering, so they stay billed at the frequent access rate. Compared with manual lifecycle rules, Intelligent-Tiering is useful when access patterns are unpredictable, since it moves objects automatically based on the last access time. Lifecycle rules give more control and no monitoring fee, and they suit data with known access patterns. Many teams combine them, using lifecycle rules for well-understood data and Intelligent-Tiering for uncertain workloads.
What causes cold starts in AWS Lambda?

A cold start happens when Lambda has to create a new execution environment to handle an invocation. This occurs when no warm environment is available, for example on the first invocation of a function, after a burst of concurrent requests that exceeds existing environments, or after a period of inactivity during which Lambda reclaims idle environments. The steps involved include provisioning a microVM through Firecracker, downloading the deployment package or container image, starting the runtime, and running the initialization code outside the handler. The total latency depends mainly on package size, runtime choice, memory allocation, and how much work happens during initialization. Warm invocations skip most of these steps and reuse the existing environment, which is why only some requests show the extra delay.
What can be done to reduce them?

Several techniques help. Keep the deployment package small by removing unused dependencies and excluding dev files. Move expensive setup such as SDK clients, database connections, and configuration loading outside the handler so it runs once per environment and is reused. Increasing the memory setting also raises the CPU share, which often shortens initialization. For latency-sensitive workloads, provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of environments initialized and ready. SnapStart, available for Java and some other runtimes, restores a snapshot of an initialized environment instead of initializing from scratch. Choosing a lighter runtime such as Node.js or Python over heavier JVM-based options can also reduce startup time.
How does provisioned concurrency differ from SnapStart?

Provisioned concurrency and SnapStart both reduce cold start impact, but they work differently. Provisioned concurrency keeps a specified number of execution environments fully initialized at all times, so requests routed to them skip initialization entirely. You pay for those environments whether or not they handle traffic. SnapStart instead takes a snapshot of an initialized environment when a function version is published, then resumes new environments from that snapshot when needed, so it does not keep environments running continuously. It is currently limited to specific runtimes and carries restrictions on certain code patterns, such as handling unique state or randomness, which may require runtime hooks to refresh after restore. Provisioned concurrency is generally better for guaranteed low latency, while SnapStart is a cost-conscious option that reduces init time without idle capacity charges.
What's the difference between Google Cloud Run and GKE?

Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that runs stateless containers and scales them automatically, including down to zero instances when idle. You deploy a container image and Google handles the servers, load balancing, and HTTPS endpoints. GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) is a managed Kubernetes service where you control clusters, node pools, networking, and the full Kubernetes API. Cloud Run trades flexibility for simplicity, while GKE gives you more control over workloads such as stateful services, DaemonSets, custom schedulers, and multi-container pod designs. Both run containers, but Cloud Run abstracts away the cluster entirely.
How does pricing compare between the two for a service that gets bursty traffic?

Cloud Run bills per request based on the vCPU and memory allocated while a request is being handled, rounded up to the nearest 100 milliseconds, plus a small charge for instances kept warm with minimum instances. When traffic is bursty and there are long idle periods, you pay little or nothing because the service can scale to zero. GKE charges for the underlying Compute Engine nodes in your cluster whether or not they are busy, plus a per-cluster management fee in Standard mode, unless you use Autopilot, which bills per pod resource request. For bursty workloads, Cloud Run usually costs less, but for steady high utilization, a well-packed GKE cluster can become cheaper per unit of compute.
What are the main limitations of Cloud Run that would push someone toward GKE?

The most common limitations are request timeouts, which cap at 60 minutes, and the lack of long-running background processes outside request handling, so workloads like persistent queues consumers or batch jobs with unusual lifecycles can be awkward. Cloud Run instances also have no persistent local disk, so stateful workloads need external storage. Networking is more constrained, with limited control over egress IP addresses without extra configuration through a VPC connector or Direct VPC egress. You also cannot run privileged containers, install custom node-level agents, or use GPUs in every region, and multi-container sidecar support is more limited than Kubernetes pod patterns. Teams needing these features typically move to GKE.
Can the two be used together in the same architecture?

Yes, and this is a common pattern. A team might run stateful databases, message brokers, or internal platform services on GKE while exposing public, stateless APIs on Cloud Run. The two can communicate over a shared VPC using private IP addressing, and Cloud Run can reach GKE services through Direct VPC egress or a serverless VPC connector. Services can also be managed with a single load balancer and Cloud Armor policies in front. Another approach is to use Cloud Run for event-driven components triggered through Eventarc or Pub/Sub, which pull from or push to workloads hosted on GKE. This hybrid approach lets each service run on the platform that fits its operational and cost profile.
What are the main types of triggers available in Azure Functions, and what does a trigger actually do?

A trigger is the event that causes a function to run. Every function has exactly one trigger, and it determines how the function is invoked and what data it receives. Common trigger types include HTTP, which runs the function when a request arrives; Timer, which runs on a schedule; Blob Storage, which fires when a blob is added or updated; Queue Storage and Service Bus, which fire when messages arrive; Event Hubs, which handles streams of events; Cosmos DB, which reacts to document changes; and Event Grid, which responds to events published by Azure services. Input and output bindings are configured separately and let the function read or write other services without custom connection code.
How does the timer trigger define its schedule, and how does it differ from a queue trigger in terms of when it runs?

The timer trigger uses an NCRONTAB expression with six fields: second, minute, hour, day, month, and day of week. For example, "0 */5 * * * *" runs every five minutes at second zero. The function runs according to the clock, whether or not any work is waiting. A queue trigger works differently: the Functions runtime polls an Azure Storage queue and invokes the function for each message it finds, so execution depends on incoming work rather than time. By default, a message that fails five times is moved to a poison queue. Service Bus triggers follow a similar pull model but add topics, subscriptions, sessions, and duplicate detection.
What's the difference between the classic blob trigger and the Event Grid based blob trigger?

The classic blob trigger works by polling the container and inspecting storage logs for changes. This approach can introduce delays, and for large containers a new blob may take several minutes to be detected. The Event Grid based blob trigger instead subscribes to blob-created events published by Azure Storage through Event Grid, so the function is invoked almost immediately after a change. It is the recommended option for most new workloads, especially when containers hold many blobs or low latency matters. It requires an Event Grid subscription, and the storage account must be configured to emit events. Both variants pass the blob contents to the function through the same binding model.
How does serverless pricing usually work for functions-as-a-service platforms?

Most function-as-a-service platforms charge based on two main dimensions: the number of invocations and the compute consumed during execution. Compute is typically measured in gigabyte-seconds, meaning the memory allocated to a function multiplied by the time it runs, often rounded up to the nearest millisecond or 100 milliseconds. Many providers also include a monthly free tier, such as a set number of requests and gigabyte-seconds, before charges begin. Some platforms add smaller fees for data transfer out, storage of deployment packages, or additional features like provisioned concurrency, which keeps instances warm and bills for idle capacity. Because you pay only for active execution, costs scale to zero when no requests arrive, though high request volumes can make the per-invocation model more expensive than reserved servers.
Why does allocated memory affect the cost of a function if the code doesn't use all of it?

On most FaaS platforms, CPU power is tied directly to the memory setting, so there is no separate CPU line item. When you increase memory, the provider proportionally allocates more compute capacity, which can shorten execution time. Billing uses the allocated amount rather than the amount actually used, so a function configured with 1 GB that only needs 200 MB is still billed for 1 GB for each second it runs. This creates a tradeoff: a higher memory setting costs more per millisecond but may finish faster, sometimes lowering the total bill. Engineers often benchmark a function at several memory sizes to find the setting with the lowest cost-per-invocation that still meets latency targets.
What's the difference between provisioned concurrency and on-demand pricing for these functions?

On-demand pricing charges only for invocations and the execution time they consume, so there is no cost when the function sits idle. Provisioned concurrency reserves a set number of initialized execution environments ahead of time. You pay a continuous hourly charge for each reserved environment whether or not it handles requests, and you also pay the usual per-invocation and duration rates when requests run on those environments. The benefit is the elimination of cold start latency, which matters for latency-sensitive APIs. The tradeoff is that it can cost more than on-demand for workloads with low or spiky traffic, so it is usually justified only when steady traffic is predictable and response time is critical. Some platforms also offer auto-scaling of the reserved count based on utilization schedules.
How do serverless database pricing models compare to function pricing?

Serverless databases often combine several metered units rather than a single compute measure. Common units include compute time measured in capacity units or request units per second, storage billed per gigabyte-month, and data transfer. Some services, such as those offering read and write request units, charge per operation with different rates for reads, writes, and strongly consistent versus eventually consistent reads. Others bill compute in fractional capacity units that scale up and down with load, sometimes with a minimum floor that prevents scaling to zero. Compared with functions, database pricing tends to have a stronger storage component and a baseline cost even when idle, because data must persist. Capacity planning therefore still matters, since bursts can consume units quickly and sustained high throughput may be cheaper on provisioned capacity.
What is a CDN and how does it work?

A content delivery network (CDN) is a geographically distributed group of servers that caches and delivers web content such as images, scripts, stylesheets, and video. When a user requests a file, DNS or anycast routing directs the request to the nearest edge server, called a point of presence (PoP). If that edge server has a fresh cached copy, it returns the file immediately. If not, it fetches the content from the origin server, stores a copy according to its cache rules, and then serves it. Because content travels a shorter distance and the origin handles fewer requests, pages load faster and the origin is better protected from traffic spikes.
How does a CDN decide how long to keep a cached file?

CDNs mainly follow the caching headers the origin sends. The Cache-Control header with a max-age or s-maxage directive sets how many seconds an edge server may store the object, with s-maxage applying only to shared caches like CDNs. The Expires header serves a similar purpose with an absolute date. If no headers are present, many CDNs fall back to a default TTL configured by the provider. Validation headers such as ETag and Last-Modified let the edge send a conditional request to the origin after the TTL expires; if the origin replies with 304 Not Modified, the cached copy is reused without re-downloading the body. Operators can also purge specific URLs or tags to remove content before its TTL ends.
How does DNS resolution work when a domain name is entered into a browser?

The browser first checks its own cache and the operating system's stub resolver checks local caches and the hosts file. If the answer isn't found locally, the stub resolver sends a query to a configured recursive resolver, usually run by an ISP or a public provider. The recursive resolver checks its cache and, if needed, queries a root server, which refers it to the appropriate top-level domain server for the name's suffix, such as .com. That TLD server returns a referral to the domain's authoritative name server, which supplies the final record, typically an A or AAAA address. The recursive resolver caches the answer for the record's TTL and returns it to the client, which then connects to the IP address.
What's the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative name server?

A recursive resolver accepts queries from clients and does the work of finding an answer. It follows referrals from root, TLD, and other servers, and it caches the results so later queries can be answered quickly. An authoritative name server holds the actual zone data for a domain, such as its A, MX, or CNAME records, and answers questions about that zone directly. It does not normally go out and query other servers on behalf of a client. In practice, one organization may run both roles, but they are separate functions, and mixing them is generally discouraged because open recursion can be abused.
Why does TTL matter in DNS caching?

TTL, or time to live, is a value in seconds attached to each record that tells resolvers how long they may cache it. It sets a trade-off between performance and freshness. A long TTL reduces query load on authoritative servers and lowers lookup latency for clients, but changes to the record take longer to propagate. A short TTL lets administrators change addresses quickly, which helps with failover, at the cost of more queries. Negative answers, such as NXDOMAIN, are also cached, with the duration usually determined by the minimum field of the zone's SOA record.
What happens if a cached record expires in the middle of a lookup?

When an entry's TTL reaches zero, the resolver must discard it and perform a fresh lookup the next time a client asks for that name. This usually means walking the delegation chain again, though the resolver can often reuse cached referrals for the parent zones, such as the TLD servers, so only the authoritative query is repeated. Some resolvers implement serve-stale behavior described in RFC 8767, returning an expired answer briefly while they refresh it in the background. This keeps names reachable when authoritative servers are temporarily unavailable, and the client may see only a small additional delay.
How does the TLS handshake work at a high level?

The TLS handshake lets a client and server agree on cryptographic parameters and establish shared keys before any application data is sent. In TLS 1.3, the client sends a ClientHello containing supported cipher suites, a random value, and its key share for an algorithm such as X25519. The server replies with a ServerHello that selects a cipher suite and its own key share. Both sides then compute a shared secret via Diffie-Hellman and derive symmetric traffic keys from it. The server sends its certificate, proving its identity, along with a CertificateVerify signature over the handshake transcript and a Finished message. The client verifies the certificate chain and signature, sends its own Finished message, and application data can then flow encrypted.
Why does the server need to sign the handshake transcript if it already sent a certificate?

The certificate only binds a public key to an identity; it does not prove that the party presenting it actually holds the matching private key. The CertificateVerify message fills that gap. The server signs a hash of the entire handshake transcript so far using its private key, and the client checks that signature against the public key in the certificate. This proves possession of the private key and ties the signature to this specific session. Because the transcript includes both key shares and random values, an attacker cannot replay an old signature into a new handshake. The Finished message then uses keys derived from the shared secret to confirm that both sides saw the same transcript, which detects any tampering with the negotiation.
What happens if the client and server cannot agree on a cipher suite during this process?

If no overlap exists between the cipher suites the client offers and those the server supports, the server cannot continue the handshake and sends a fatal handshake_failure alert, after which the connection closes. In TLS 1.3, the server must choose from the client's offered list, so the failure is explicit. Older versions had more negotiation paths, and implementations sometimes had downgrade risks, which is why TLS 1.3 protects the negotiation by including the advertised parameters in the transcript covered by the Finished messages. If an attacker altered the ClientHello to remove strong options, the mismatch would cause the Finished verification to fail on at least one side, so the connection aborts rather than silently using weaker settings.
What are the main assumptions behind ordinary least squares linear regression?

The classical assumptions are usually listed as follows. First, linearity: the expected value of the response is a linear function of the predictors, with parameters entering additively. Second, independence: the errors are independent of one another, which is often violated in time series or clustered data. Third, homoscedasticity: the error variance is constant across all levels of the predictors. Fourth, normality of errors: the residuals are normally distributed, which matters mainly for valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests in small samples. Fifth, no perfect multicollinearity: no predictor is an exact linear combination of others, so the design matrix has full column rank. Finally, exogeneity: the errors have zero conditional mean given the predictors, meaning no omitted variables correlated with the regressors and no measurement error in them. Violating exogeneity biases the coefficient estimates, while violating the others mainly affects efficiency and inference.
Why does violating exogeneity bias the coefficients, while the other violations don't?

Exogeneity is what makes the OLS estimator unbiased. The estimator can be written as beta-hat equals beta plus (X'X) inverse X'e. If the errors e are correlated with X, the term X'e does not average to zero, so the estimate is systematically off, and more data does not fix this because the bias persists asymptotically. Violations of homoscedasticity or independence leave the estimator unbiased and consistent but make the usual standard errors wrong, so t-tests and confidence intervals become unreliable. The estimator is still correct on average; it is just no longer the most efficient, and its reported uncertainty is misstated. Non-normality is less serious still, since by the central limit theorem the coefficient estimates are approximately normal in large samples anyway.
How can I check whether homoscedasticity holds in practice?

The most common approach is to plot residuals against fitted values. If the spread of residuals forms a funnel or fan shape, the variance is likely changing with the mean. A formal check is the Breusch-Pagan test, which regresses the squared residuals on the predictors and tests whether they explain variation; a small p-value indicates heteroscedasticity. White's test is a more general version that also includes squared terms and interactions, so it detects a wider range of patterns but uses more degrees of freedom. If heteroscedasticity is present, one remedy is to use heteroscedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors, such as HC3, which keep the coefficient estimates but correct their standard errors. Another option is a weighted least squares model or a transformation of the response, such as taking logs, when the variance grows with the mean.
If I use robust standard errors, do I still need to worry about multicollinearity?

Yes. Robust standard errors correct for heteroscedasticity in the estimated variance of the coefficients, but they do not remove the underlying problem. When predictors are highly correlated, the matrix X'X is nearly singular, so the coefficient estimates have large variances and can change dramatically with small changes in the data. Robust errors will reflect this larger uncertainty, but the wide intervals still mean the individual coefficients are hard to interpret. Perfect multicollinearity is a different matter: the model cannot be estimated at all, and software will typically drop a variable or return an error. To diagnose near-collinearity, examine the variance inflation factor, where values above roughly 5 to 10 are often flagged, or check condition indices. Remedies include removing or combining redundant predictors, centering variables, or using regularization such as ridge regression.
What's the difference between logistic regression and decision trees for classification?

Logistic regression is a linear model. It estimates the log-odds of a class as a weighted sum of input features, then passes that through the sigmoid function to produce a probability. Its decision boundary is a hyperplane in feature space, so it works well when classes are roughly linearly separable and when you want interpretable coefficients that show how each feature shifts the odds. Decision trees instead split the feature space with a sequence of axis-aligned threshold rules, such as "income > 50k" then "age < 30". Each leaf predicts a class, usually the majority class of training samples that reach it. Trees capture nonlinear interactions and thresholds automatically, but a single deep tree tends to overfit and is sensitive to small changes in the data.
Given that trees can overfit, how do people usually control that, and does logistic regression have a similar issue?

For trees, the usual controls are limiting max depth, requiring a minimum number of samples per split or leaf, and pruning after growth using cost-complexity pruning. Ensembles such as random forests and gradient boosting reduce variance further by averaging or sequentially correcting many trees. Logistic regression overfits differently. With many features relative to samples, or with highly correlated predictors, its coefficients become unstable and can blow up, particularly when classes are perfectly separable, where maximum likelihood estimates diverge. The standard remedy is L2 or L1 regularization, which shrinks coefficients and, with L1, can zero out irrelevant features. So both models need regularization, but trees are controlled through structure limits while logistic regression is controlled through penalties on its weights.
In practice, when would you pick one over the other based on the data you have?

Logistic regression is a strong choice when the number of features is large relative to observations, when relationships are close to additive and roughly linear in the log-odds, when you need calibrated probabilities that are easy to explain, or when regulators or stakeholders require coefficient-level transparency. It also trains quickly and is robust with sparse, high-dimensional inputs such as text counts. Decision trees are preferable when relationships involve strong interactions or nonlinear thresholds, when features are a mix of numeric and categorical types with little preprocessing, when missing values are common, or when feature scaling is inconvenient. Trees need no scaling and handle monotone transformations naturally. A practical approach is to fit both as baselines, compare them with cross-validation, and check calibration before choosing.
What does overfitting mean in machine learning, and how can you tell when it is happening?

Overfitting happens when a model learns the noise and idiosyncrasies of its training data instead of the underlying pattern, so it performs very well on the examples it has seen but poorly on new data. The most common sign is a gap between training and validation performance: training loss keeps falling while validation loss starts rising after some point. Learning curves make this visible, since the two curves diverge as training continues. Another signal is a model with far more parameters than the dataset can reasonably support, such as a deep network trained on a few hundred examples. Checking accuracy on a held-out set, rather than only on training data, is the practical way to catch it.
What are the main regularization techniques that help with that, and how do they differ?

The main techniques fall into a few families. L2 regularization (weight decay) adds a penalty proportional to the squared size of the weights, which discourages any single weight from growing large and tends to spread importance across features. L1 regularization adds a penalty on the absolute values of weights, which pushes many weights to exactly zero and yields sparse models useful for feature selection. Dropout randomly zeros a fraction of neuron activations during each training step, forcing the network not to rely on specific units. Early stopping halts training once validation loss stops improving. Data augmentation and limiting model capacity are further options. L1 and L2 act directly on the loss, while dropout and early stopping act on the training process itself.
How do you choose the strength of an L2 penalty in practice?

The penalty strength, usually written as lambda or alpha, is a hyperparameter that is chosen by validation rather than set by theory. A common approach is to define a logarithmic grid, such as values from 1e-5 to 1e2 in powers of ten, train a model for each value, and record validation error. Plotting validation error against lambda typically shows a U-shape: very small values leave the model overfitting, while very large values underfit by shrinking weights too aggressively. Cross-validation gives more reliable estimates when data is limited. Once a rough region is found, a finer search around it refines the choice. The final model is then evaluated once on a separate test set to confirm the chosen value generalizes.
Does regularization always improve generalization, or can it hurt in some cases?

Regularization does not always help. When a model is already underfitting, adding a penalty removes capacity it needs, so both training and validation error stay high. Very strong regularization can push weights toward zero so that predictions collapse toward a trivial baseline. Some regularizers also interact badly with the data: L1 penalties may arbitrarily select one of several correlated features, and heavy dropout can slow convergence enough to hurt final accuracy within a fixed training budget. Regularization also assumes the penalty matches a reasonable prior about the solution, so a mismatched penalty can bias the model. The right amount depends on the dataset size, noise level, and model capacity, which is why tuning against validation performance remains essential.
How does k-fold cross-validation work?

In k-fold cross-validation, the dataset is randomly partitioned into k roughly equal subsets, called folds. The model is trained k times. In each round, one fold is held out as the validation set and the remaining k-1 folds form the training set. After training, the model is scored on the held-out fold. Once all k rounds are complete, you have k performance scores, and you typically report their mean and standard deviation. Common choices are k=5 or k=10. Every observation is used for validation exactly once, which gives a more stable estimate of generalization error than a single train-test split, though it costs roughly k times the training computation.
What's the difference between that and stratified k-fold?

Standard k-fold splits the data at random, so for imbalanced classification some folds may contain very few examples of a minority class, or none at all. Stratified k-fold fixes this by preserving the class proportions in each fold. For example, if 10% of labels are positive in the full dataset, each fold will contain approximately 10% positives. This makes the validation scores less noisy and avoids folds where metrics like recall or precision are undefined. Stratification is the default in scikit-learn's StratifiedKFold and is commonly used for classification. For regression, a similar idea can be applied by stratifying on binned target values.
When would I need something like leave-one-out or time series splits instead?

Leave-one-out cross-validation is a special case where k equals the number of samples, so each observation serves once as the validation set. It is nearly unbiased but expensive, and its scores tend to have high variance because the training sets overlap heavily. It can be useful with very small datasets. Time series splits are needed when observations are ordered in time and future data should not influence training. Methods like scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit create expanding training windows, where each validation fold comes strictly after its training data. Random shuffling in this setting would leak future information into the past and produce overly optimistic estimates.
What do precision, recall, and F1 score actually measure in a classification model?

Precision, recall, and F1 are metrics derived from the confusion matrix, which counts true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive: TP / (TP + FP). It answers the question, of the items the model flagged, how many were correct. Recall, also called sensitivity or true positive rate, is the fraction of actual positives the model found: TP / (TP + FN). It answers, of all the real positives, how many did the model catch. F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 × (precision × recall) / (precision + recall). It summarizes both into a single number and is only high when both values are reasonably high.
Why use a harmonic mean for F1 instead of a simple average of precision and recall?

The harmonic mean punishes imbalance much more than the arithmetic mean. Consider a model with precision 1.0 and recall 0.01. The arithmetic mean is 0.505, which suggests moderate performance, but the F1 score is about 0.02. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot score well by excelling at one metric while neglecting the other. For example, a model that labels everything as positive gets recall 1.0 but may have very low precision, and its F1 will reflect that weakness. This property makes F1 useful as a balanced summary when neither metric should be sacrificed for the other.
How do you choose between optimizing for precision or recall in a given problem?

The choice depends on the relative cost of the two error types. Favor recall when missing a positive is costly, such as screening for a serious disease or detecting fraud in a safety-critical system, since false negatives are the dangerous outcome. Favor precision when false alarms are costly, such as flagging legitimate emails as spam or triggering expensive manual reviews, because each false positive wastes resources or frustrates people. Practically, most classifiers output a probability or score, and you pick a decision threshold. Raising the threshold generally increases precision and decreases recall, while lowering it does the reverse. You can plot precision against recall across thresholds on a precision-recall curve and choose the operating point that matches the business or safety requirements.
When would F1 be misleading, and what alternatives exist for those cases?

F1 can mislead when true negatives matter or when classes are highly imbalanced in ways that change the task. Because F1 ignores true negatives, a model can look good on F1 while performing poorly at rejecting negatives, which matters in some medical or quality-control settings. F1 also treats precision and recall as equally important, which may not reflect the actual costs. Alternatives include the F-beta score, where beta above one weights recall more heavily and beta below one weights precision more heavily. Matthews correlation coefficient uses all four confusion matrix cells and is more informative under heavy imbalance. For multiclass problems, macro-averaged F1 gives each class equal weight, while micro-averaged F1 weights by instance count. Area under the precision-recall curve is another threshold-independent summary worth reporting alongside F1.
How does a ROC curve work?

A ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic curve) plots the true positive rate (sensitivity) against the false positive rate (1 minus specificity) for a binary classifier across all possible decision thresholds. Each threshold turns the model's predicted scores into positive or negative labels, producing one (FPR, TPR) point. Lowering the threshold classifies more cases as positive, which raises both TPR and FPR; raising it does the opposite. Connecting the points from the strictest threshold (near 0,0) to the most lenient (near 1,1) gives the curve. A perfect classifier passes through the top-left corner (0,1), while a random classifier produces a diagonal line from (0,0) to (1,1). The curve therefore shows the trade-off between catching positives and falsely flagging negatives, without committing to a single threshold.
What does the AUC actually measure?

AUC stands for area under the ROC curve, and it summarizes the curve as a single number between 0 and 1. A useful interpretation is probabilistic: AUC equals the probability that the model assigns a higher score to a randomly chosen positive example than to a randomly chosen negative example. An AUC of 0.5 corresponds to random ranking, the diagonal line, while 1.0 means every positive is ranked above every negative. Values below 0.5 indicate the model ranks in the wrong direction, though flipping its predictions would usually fix that. Because AUC depends only on how scores are ordered, it is unaffected by the choice of threshold and by any monotonic transformation of the scores. It does not reflect calibration, meaning whether predicted probabilities match actual frequencies.
When would AUC be a misleading metric to rely on?

AUC can mislead when the class distribution is heavily imbalanced. Because the false positive rate is computed relative to the large negative class, a model can achieve a high AUC while still producing many false positives in absolute terms, which matters when positives are rare. In such cases a precision-recall curve and its average precision often give a more informative picture. AUC also weights all regions of the curve equally, so a model may score well overall while performing poorly in the low-FPR region that a practical application requires. Partial AUC over a restricted false positive range can address this. Finally, AUC says nothing about the costs of different errors or the threshold you will actually deploy, so it should be paired with metrics at a chosen operating point.
What's the difference between batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent?

The three variants differ in how many training examples they use to estimate the gradient for each parameter update. Batch gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire training set before taking one step. It gives a precise gradient direction but each update is expensive on large datasets. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses a single randomly chosen example per update. Updates are cheap and noisy, which can help escape shallow local minima but makes convergence oscillate. Mini-batch gradient descent is the common compromise: it averages the gradient over a small subset, typically 32 to 512 examples. This exploits vectorized hardware efficiently while keeping enough averaging to stabilize training.
Why does momentum help with those noisy updates, and how is it usually added?

Momentum keeps an exponentially decaying average of past gradients and moves parameters along that average rather than the raw current gradient. The update is v = beta * v + gradient, then theta = theta - learning_rate * v, with beta commonly set to 0.9. Noisy components of the gradient that change sign from step to step partially cancel out in the average, while consistent components accumulate and speed up progress. This smooths the oscillations typical of mini-batch SGD, especially along narrow, steep valleys where the loss curves sharply in one direction and slowly in another. Nesterov momentum is a variant that evaluates the gradient after applying the velocity step, often giving slightly faster convergence.
How do adaptive methods like Adagrad and Adam differ from plain momentum?

Momentum uses one global learning rate for all parameters, while adaptive methods scale the step size for each parameter individually. Adagrad accumulates the sum of squared gradients for each parameter and divides the learning rate by its square root. Parameters with frequently large gradients receive smaller steps, which suits sparse features, but the accumulated sum only grows, so the effective learning rate can shrink too much over long training. RMSprop fixes this by using an exponentially decaying average of squared gradients. Adam combines this with momentum: it tracks a decaying average of gradients (first moment) and of squared gradients (second moment), applies bias correction for their initialization at zero, and then updates using their ratio. Its default settings, such as beta1 of 0.9 and beta2 of 0.999, work well across many problems.
When would someone choose SGD with momentum over Adam, and what are the tradeoffs?

Adam often converges quickly with little tuning, which makes it a strong default, but tuned SGD with momentum frequently reaches better final generalization on some tasks, particularly large-scale image classification. One explanation is that Adam's per-parameter scaling can lead it toward sharper minima that generalize less well, though this is debated and depends on the setup. SGD with momentum has fewer state variables, using one velocity buffer per parameter instead of two, so it uses less memory. Its main drawback is sensitivity to the learning rate, which usually requires a schedule such as cosine decay or step decay. Adam is also more forgiving when gradients vary greatly in scale across layers, such as in transformers. In practice, many practitioners try both and select based on validation performance.
How does batch normalization work in neural networks?

Batch normalization normalizes the inputs to a layer using statistics computed over the current mini-batch. For each feature, it subtracts the batch mean and divides by the batch standard deviation, producing values with roughly zero mean and unit variance. It then applies two learnable parameters per feature, a scale (gamma) and a shift (beta), so the network can recover whatever distribution is actually useful, including the identity transform if needed. During training, the batch statistics are used; at inference, the layer uses running averages of the mean and variance accumulated during training, so predictions don't depend on batch composition. This normalization typically sits between a linear or convolutional layer and its activation function.
Why does normalizing activations help training speed up?

The original motivation was reducing internal covariate shift, meaning the distribution of each layer's inputs changes as earlier layer weights update. Keeping those distributions stable lets each layer learn more independently and allows higher learning rates without divergence. More recent work suggests a different main effect: batch normalization smooths the loss landscape, making gradients more predictable and the optimization surface less sharp. It also reduces sensitivity to weight initialization and scale. Because the normalized values stay in a range where activation functions like sigmoid or tanh have meaningful gradients, saturation is less likely. These properties together usually mean fewer epochs to reach a given loss.
What are the main drawbacks, and when would someone choose layer normalization instead?

The biggest drawback is its dependence on batch size. With very small batches, the mean and variance estimates become noisy, which degrades accuracy, and the train-versus-inference discrepancy grows. It also complicates recurrent networks, where statistics vary across time steps, and distributed training requires synchronizing statistics across devices. Layer normalization addresses these issues by computing mean and variance across the features of a single example rather than across the batch. Because it is independent of batch size and behaves identically in training and inference, it is common in transformers and sequence models. Batch normalization generally remains the default for convolutional networks trained with reasonably large batches.
What is dropout in neural networks and why is it used?

Dropout is a regularization technique where, during training, each neuron's output is set to zero with some probability p, commonly 0.5 for hidden layers and around 0.2 for input layers. This prevents units from co-adapting, which forces the network to learn more redundant and robust features. It reduces overfitting by approximating an ensemble of many thinned versions of the network that share weights. At inference time, dropout is turned off. Most frameworks use inverted dropout, which scales the surviving activations by 1/(1-p) during training so that no adjustment is needed at test time.
How does inverted dropout differ from the original formulation?

The original dropout method from Hinton and colleagues kept all neurons during training with probability 1-p and then multiplied the weights by (1-p) at test time. Inverted dropout moves that scaling into the training step: kept activations are divided by (1-p) during training. The forward pass at inference is then just the standard network with no extra multiplication. Mathematically the two approaches are equivalent in expectation. Inverted dropout is the version implemented in PyTorch and TensorFlow because it keeps deployment code simple and avoids modifying trained weights after training.
Are there situations where dropout tends to hurt performance?

Yes. Dropout often helps less in convolutional layers, because neighboring spatial features are highly correlated and remain informative even when some are removed. Combining dropout with batch normalization can cause a variance shift between training and inference that degrades results. Very large models trained on abundant data may not need it at all. Recurrent networks also require variational dropout, which uses the same mask across time steps; applying independent masks at each step disrupts the hidden state's memory. Using too high a rate on a small network can cause underfitting.
What are some alternatives or complements to dropout for regularization?

Common alternatives include L2 weight decay, which penalizes large weights, and early stopping, which halts training when validation loss begins to rise. Data augmentation expands the training set with transformed examples, such as crops or flips for images. Batch normalization has a mild regularizing effect on its own. DropConnect drops individual weights rather than activations. Label smoothing softens target labels to reduce overconfidence, and stochastic depth randomly skips residual blocks during training, which is useful in very deep networks. These methods are often combined, and the best mix depends on dataset size and architecture.
How does a convolutional neural network actually process an image?

A convolutional neural network processes an image by sliding small learnable filters, usually 3x3 or 5x5, across the input. At each position, the filter multiplies its weights with the underlying pixel values and sums them to produce one number. Repeating this across the whole image produces a feature map that highlights where a particular pattern, such as an edge or a color transition, appears. A layer typically applies many filters in parallel, so it outputs a stack of feature maps. Early layers tend to detect simple edges and textures, while deeper layers combine these into more complex shapes and object parts. Pooling layers and nonlinear activations such as ReLU are usually interleaved between convolutions to reduce spatial resolution and add expressiveness.
What is the difference between pooling and using a strided convolution to downsample?

Both reduce spatial resolution, but they differ in whether they have learnable parameters. Max pooling or average pooling uses a fixed operation over a small window, such as taking the maximum value in each 2x2 region, and has no weights to train. A strided convolution moves its filter in steps larger than one pixel, so it skips positions while still computing a learned weighted sum. This means a strided convolution can learn what information to keep when downsampling, whereas pooling applies the same rule everywhere. Pooling provides a small amount of built-in translation invariance and is computationally cheap. Many modern architectures, including some well-known image classifiers, replace pooling with strided convolutions to simplify the network and let the downsampling be learned from data.
Given that deeper layers see larger regions of the input, how is that receptive field size calculated?

The receptive field of a neuron is the region of the original input that influences its value. For a stack of convolutional layers, it can be computed layer by layer. If the current receptive field is r, the previous layers' stride product is j, and a new layer has kernel size k and stride s, then the new receptive field is r + (k - 1) times j. The stride product j is updated by multiplying by s after each layer. For example, three stacked 3x3 convolutions with stride 1 give a receptive field of 7x7, since each layer adds 2 pixels. Dilated convolutions and pooling increase the receptive field faster without adding as many parameters, which is why deep networks can integrate context across large parts of an image.
How do recurrent neural networks process sequences differently from feedforward networks?

A feedforward network maps a fixed-size input to an output in a single pass, with no memory of previous inputs. A recurrent neural network (RNN) instead processes a sequence one element at a time and maintains a hidden state vector that is updated at each step. At time step t, the hidden state h_t is computed from the current input x_t and the previous hidden state h_{t-1}, typically as h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1} + b). The same weights are reused at every time step, which lets the network handle sequences of varying length and carry information forward. The output at each step can be read from h_t, and the whole chain can be unrolled through time for training with backpropagation through time.
Why do plain RNNs struggle with long sequences?

The main problem is the vanishing and exploding gradient problem. During backpropagation through time, the gradient of the loss with respect to early hidden states is a product of many Jacobian matrices, one per time step. If these factors have norms below one, the gradient shrinks exponentially and the network stops learning dependencies that span many steps. If the norms are above one, the gradients grow exponentially and training becomes unstable. Gradient clipping addresses exploding gradients fairly well, but vanishing gradients are harder to fix within the basic architecture. In practice, this means a vanilla RNN tends to capture only short-range patterns, even though in principle its hidden state could retain longer context.
How do LSTMs address the vanishing gradient problem?

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks add a separate cell state c_t that flows through time with only elementwise operations, which creates a near-linear path for gradients. Three gates control this flow. The forget gate f_t = sigmoid(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) decides what to erase from the cell state, the input gate i_t decides how much of a candidate value to write, and the output gate o_t decides how much of the cell state is exposed as the hidden state h_t = o_t * tanh(c_t). Because the cell update is c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * g_t, the gradient through the cell is multiplied by the forget gate rather than repeatedly by a weight matrix. When f_t is close to one, information and gradients can persist across many steps.
What are common variants of the LSTM, and how do they differ?

The most widely used variant is the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), which merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate z_t and adds a reset gate r_t that controls how much of the previous hidden state is used when forming the candidate. GRUs have no separate cell state and fewer parameters, so they train faster and often perform comparably on smaller datasets. Other variants include peephole connections, where gates also read the cell state, and bidirectional LSTMs, which run one LSTM forward and another backward over the sequence and concatenate their outputs. Stacked LSTMs add depth by feeding one layer's hidden states into the next. The choice between them is usually made empirically, since differences in accuracy depend heavily on the task.

topic: the transformer architecture at a high level

turns.text: How does the transformer architecture work at a high level?

A transformer is a neural network that processes a whole sequence at once rather than one token at a time, as recurrent networks did. Its core idea is self-attention: each token's representation is updated by computing weighted combinations of all the other tokens' representations. The weights come from comparing learned query and key vectors, and the weighted sum uses value vectors. The model is built from stacked blocks, each containing a multi-head self-attention layer and a position-wise feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalization around each sublayer. Because attention itself has no notion of order, positional encodings are added to the input embeddings so the model knows where each token sits in the sequence.
Why do they use multiple attention heads instead of just one?

Multiple heads let the model attend to different kinds of relationships in parallel. Each head has its own query, key, and value projections, so it can learn a separate pattern of interaction. One head might track syntactic dependencies between nearby words, while another captures coreference across a longer span. The input is projected into several lower-dimensional subspaces, each head computes attention within its subspace, and the outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension. The total computation is roughly the same as a single full-dimensional head, so the benefit comes from diversity of representation rather than extra cost.
How does the decoder side differ from the encoder side?

The encoder stack uses bidirectional self-attention, so every token can attend to every other token in the input. The decoder stack is autoregressive: during training it uses a causal mask so each position can only attend to earlier positions, which prevents it from seeing the answers it is meant to predict. Decoder blocks also include a cross-attention sublayer, where queries come from the decoder and keys and values come from the encoder output. This lets the decoder condition on the full source sequence at each generation step. Some models, such as GPT-style language models, use only the decoder stack, while others such as BERT use only the encoder.
How does the computational complexity of self-attention scale with sequence length?

Standard self-attention computes a score for every pair of positions in the sequence. For a sequence of length n with model dimension d, forming the query-key product QK^T produces an n by n matrix, which requires O(n^2 d) multiplications. Applying the softmax to that matrix costs O(n^2), and multiplying the attention weights by the value matrix V costs another O(n^2 d). Overall time complexity is therefore O(n^2 d). The memory needed to store the full attention matrix is O(n^2) per head, which often becomes the practical bottleneck before raw compute does, since doubling the sequence length quadruples this memory footprint.
Why does the memory cost often matter more than the arithmetic cost in practice?

Modern accelerators such as GPUs can perform arithmetic very quickly, but moving data between high-bandwidth memory and on-chip SRAM is comparatively slow. Standard attention writes the full n by n score matrix to high-bandwidth memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the result, and reads it again for the value multiplication. These repeated reads and writes make the operation memory-bound rather than compute-bound. As a result, the wall-clock time and maximum feasible sequence length are limited by memory traffic and capacity, even when the number of floating-point operations is manageable.
What approaches exist for reducing the quadratic cost of attention?

Several families of methods address this. Sparse attention restricts each position to attend to a fixed or learned subset of others, such as local windows or strided patterns, reducing cost toward O(n sqrt(n)) or O(n w) for window size w. Low-rank and kernel-based methods, such as Linformer and Performer, approximate the softmax attention matrix so the cost becomes linear in n, at some cost in accuracy. Recurrence-based approaches, like Transformer-XL segment recurrence, reuse hidden states across chunks. Finally, IO-aware exact methods such as FlashAttention keep the O(n^2) arithmetic but tile the computation so the full matrix is never materialized in slow memory, yielding large speedups and linear memory use.
How does FlashAttention avoid materializing the full matrix while still computing an exact softmax?

It relies on tiling and an online softmax algorithm. Queries, keys, and values are split into blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM. For each query block, the kernel iterates over key and value blocks, computing a partial score tile. Because softmax requires a row-wise maximum and normalizer, FlashAttention maintains running statistics: the current maximum m and sum of exponentials l for each row. When a new block arrives, it rescales the previously accumulated output and normalizer using the updated maximum, so the final result is mathematically identical to full softmax. The backward pass recomputes attention tiles from stored softmax statistics instead of saving the n by n matrix, trading some extra computation for much less memory traffic.
What's the difference between absolute and relative positional encodings in transformers?

Absolute positional encodings assign each token position a fixed vector based on its index in the sequence. The original Transformer used sinusoidal functions of different frequencies, while BERT learned a separate embedding for each position up to a maximum length. The model adds these vectors to the token embeddings, so attention scores depend on absolute indices. Relative encodings instead model the distance between a query and a key position. Shaw et al. added learned relative offsets directly into the attention computation, and T5 used simple learned scalar biases indexed by clipped relative distance. Because the signal depends on offsets rather than absolute locations, relative schemes often generalize better to sequences longer than those seen during training.
Why do sinusoidal encodings allow the model to reason about relative offsets, even though they are absolute?

For any fixed offset k, the encoding at position pos+k can be written as a linear transformation of the encoding at pos. Each pair of dimensions contains a sine and cosine at frequency omega, and shifting the position by k rotates that pair by angle omega times k. The rotation matrix depends only on k, not on pos. Since attention computes dot products between queries and keys, a linear layer can in principle learn to extract these shifts and compare positions by their gap. The frequencies form a geometric progression from 2 pi to roughly 10000 times 2 pi, so different dimensions capture short and long distances. This property is useful, but in practice the learned mapping is imperfect, and models trained with sinusoids do not always extrapolate well beyond their training length.
How do rotary embeddings build on that idea, and why have they become popular in large language models?

Rotary Position Embedding, or RoPE, applies the rotation directly to the query and key vectors rather than adding a signal to the input. The vector is split into two-dimensional pairs, and each pair is rotated by an angle proportional to the token position, using frequencies similar to the sinusoidal scheme. When the query at position m and key at position n are dot-multiplied, the result depends only on the difference m minus n. This gives relative behavior without extra parameters or changes to the attention score formula. RoPE is cheap to compute and works well with caching of keys. Methods such as position interpolation and NTK-aware scaling adjust the rotation frequencies to extend context length after training, which is a major reason RoPE appears in many widely used open models.
How does byte-level BPE tokenization work at a high level?

Byte-level BPE starts from a base vocabulary of exactly 256 symbols, one for each possible byte value. Text is first encoded to UTF-8, so every character becomes one or more bytes, and the training corpus is represented as a sequence of these byte symbols. The algorithm then counts all adjacent symbol pairs in the corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new symbol, adds that symbol to the vocabulary, and rewrites the corpus with the merge applied. This counting-and-merging step repeats until the vocabulary reaches a target size, such as 50,000 entries. The learned merge rules are stored in order, and at inference time they are applied in the same order to split new text into tokens.
Why do byte-level models start from bytes instead of characters?

Starting from bytes guarantees that the base vocabulary covers any input without an unknown-token fallback, because every string is representable as a sequence of the 256 byte values.
