Character-level starting points would need thousands of symbols to cover Unicode scripts, and rare characters would appear too seldom to learn good merges. Bytes keep the initial vocabulary small and fixed. The tradeoff is that a single non-ASCII character can occupy two to four bytes, so non-English text may split into more tokens than the same text in English, and some merges can produce fragments that are not valid characters on their own.
What happens when a merge produces a partial UTF-8 sequence?

The merge still happens, since the algorithm only sees byte values and frequency counts. A token can therefore hold an incomplete multibyte character, for example the first byte of a three-byte character without its continuation bytes. Such a token is not a valid string when decoded alone. This is handled at decode time: the decoder concatenates the raw bytes of all tokens first and only then interprets the result as UTF-8, so the complete character is reassembled correctly across token boundaries. Problems arise only if a generation stops mid-character, in which case the output may contain replacement characters until the remaining bytes arrive.
How do pre-tokenization rules interact with byte-level BPE?

Most implementations apply a pre-tokenization step before BPE merges are performed. A regular expression splits the raw text into chunks, such as words, numbers, punctuation runs, and whitespace-prefixed words. BPE merges are then learned and applied only within each chunk, so no merge can cross a chunk boundary. This prevents tokens from combining the end of one word with the start of the next and keeps frequent words stable. GPT-2 used a pattern that attaches leading spaces to the following word, so a word like ' the' has its own token. Changing this regex changes the vocabulary and the segmentation of every input, so it is fixed once the tokenizer is trained.
What's the difference between word embeddings and contextual embeddings?

Word embeddings assign each word a single fixed vector regardless of where it appears. Methods like Word2Vec (skip-gram and CBOW) and GloVe learn these vectors from co-occurrence statistics across a large corpus, so the word "bank" gets one representation that blends its financial and river meanings. Contextual embeddings, produced by models such as ELMo and BERT, compute a vector for each token based on the surrounding sentence. The same word therefore receives different vectors in "river bank" and "bank account," because the representation depends on the full input sequence rather than a lookup table.
How are those contextual vectors actually computed inside a model like BERT?

BERT is a stack of Transformer encoder layers. The input begins with token embeddings, position embeddings, and segment embeddings, which are summed. Each layer then applies multi-head self-attention, where every token forms query, key, and value vectors and attends to all other tokens in the sequence, followed by a feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalization around each sublayer. Because attention mixes information across positions, the output vector for a token at the final layer encodes its meaning in context. Researchers often use the hidden states from the last layer, or a weighted combination of several layers, as the contextual embedding for downstream tasks.
Can you use a static word embedding and a contextual one together, or do you have to pick one?

You can combine them, and this is a common strategy when training data is limited. One approach is to concatenate a static vector, such as GloVe, with the contextual vector from BERT for each token before passing them to a classifier. Another is to use the static embeddings to initialize the input layer of a model that then learns contextual representations on top. Some studies have found that static embeddings still add value for rare words, since their vectors are learned from very large corpora and are less affected by noisy context in a small task dataset. The tradeoff is extra memory and a more complex pipeline, so the choice usually depends on the task size and the computational budget.
What's the difference between cosine similarity and dot product?

The dot product of two vectors is the sum of the products of their corresponding components, a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ. It depends on both direction and magnitude, so longer vectors produce larger values even if they point the same way. Cosine similarity normalizes that away: it equals the dot product divided by the product of the vectors' lengths, cos(θ) = (a·b) / (‖a‖‖b‖). The result always falls between -1 and 1, and it measures only the angle between the vectors. Cosine similarity is therefore the dot product of the unit-normalized versions of the two vectors.
When would I actually prefer the raw dot product over cosine similarity?

The raw dot product is useful when magnitude carries meaningful information. For example, in recommender systems, a user embedding's norm can reflect how strongly someone engages with items, and a dot product score between user and item embeddings naturally captures both relevance and confidence. Many matrix factorization models and neural ranking models are trained with dot product scoring for this reason. Cosine similarity is preferred when you only care about orientation, such as comparing document embeddings of different lengths or text representations where vector norms are noisy artifacts of training. Using cosine in those cases avoids letting long or frequent items dominate simply because their vectors are larger.
If I normalize all my vectors to unit length first, does the choice between the two still matter?

No, once every vector has unit length, the two metrics become mathematically identical. Since ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 1, the cosine formula reduces to just a·b. Rankings produced by dot product and cosine will therefore match exactly for any query against a fixed set of normalized vectors. This is why many systems normalize embeddings at indexing time and then use the faster dot product operation, which is well supported by approximate nearest neighbor libraries. The choice still matters for the vectors you have not normalized, and normalizing changes what the score means, so you should be consistent between training and inference.
Are there cases where cosine similarity gives a misleading result?

Yes, a few. Cosine similarity ignores magnitude entirely, so two vectors pointing in nearly the same direction score highly even if one has a very small norm built from noise or sparse evidence. In word embeddings, rare words often have smaller norms and less reliable directions, so cosine can overweight them. Cosine also treats all dimensions equally after normalization, so a few dimensions with large values can dominate the angle. Another issue is that cosine is not a true distance metric in the strict sense when used directly, since 1 minus cosine does not satisfy the triangle inequality, though the angular distance arccos(cos θ) does. Checking whether magnitude is informative for your data is a practical way to decide.
How does HNSW work for approximate nearest neighbor search?

HNSW, or Hierarchical Navigable Small World, builds a multi-layer graph over the vectors. Each element is assigned a maximum layer at random, with higher layers becoming exponentially sparser, similar to a skip list. The top layer has few nodes and long-range links, which let a search make large jumps toward the query. Lower layers are denser and have short-range links for fine-grained refinement. A query enters at the top layer, greedily moves to the closest node, then descends one layer at a time, using the closest node found as the entry point for the next layer. At layer zero, a beam search keeps a candidate list of size ef and returns the k best matches. Larger ef improves recall at the cost of latency.
What do the M and efConstruction parameters control when building the index?

M sets the maximum number of bidirectional links each node keeps per layer; layer zero typically allows 2M links. Higher M gives a better-connected graph and higher recall, but increases memory use and build time. efConstruction sets the size of the dynamic candidate list used while inserting each new element. When a new node is inserted, the algorithm searches for its neighbors with this beam width, then selects up to M of them using a heuristic that favors diverse directions rather than just the nearest points. A larger efConstruction produces a higher-quality graph and better recall at query time, but slows indexing. Both parameters are fixed once the graph is built, so they are chosen with the recall and memory targets in mind.
What are the main trade-offs of HNSW compared with inverted-file or product quantization methods?

HNSW typically delivers very high recall and low query latency, since its graph search touches relatively few distance computations. Its main drawback is memory: each vector is stored in full precision along with its graph links, often requiring several times the raw data size. Inverted-file methods such as IVF partition vectors into clusters and search only the nearest clusters, which uses less memory and suits very large datasets, though recall depends on how many clusters are probed. Product quantization compresses vectors into short codes, drastically reducing memory, but introduces approximation error in distances. Many production systems combine these ideas, for example IVF with PQ for memory savings, or HNSW over compressed vectors, to balance recall, latency, and footprint. Insertion and deletion also differ: HNSW supports incremental inserts well, while IVF centroids may need periodic retraining.
What's the difference between a vector database and a traditional relational database for similarity search?

A relational database stores structured rows and answers exact-match or range queries using B-tree indexes. A vector database is built to store high-dimensional embeddings, which are arrays of floating-point numbers produced by machine learning models, and to find the nearest neighbors to a query vector. It relies on approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes such as HNSW, IVF, or product quantization, which trade a small amount of recall for large gains in speed. Relational systems can store vectors and compute distances, often with extensions like pgvector, but exhaustive distance computation over millions of rows becomes slow without specialized indexing. Vector databases also typically handle metadata filtering alongside similarity ranking, which is the core workload they are optimized for.
How does HNSW compare with IVF indexing in terms of memory use and query speed?

HNSW, or Hierarchical Navigable Small World, builds a multi-layer graph where each vector links to several neighbors, and search greedily traverses that graph from coarse upper layers down to dense base layers. It usually delivers high recall at low latency, but the graph links add substantial memory overhead, often well above the raw vector size, and index builds are slower. IVF, or inverted file index, clusters vectors with k-means and at query time scans only the nearest few clusters, specified by an nprobe parameter. It uses less memory and builds faster, but recall depends heavily on how many clusters are probed, so it generally needs more tuning to match HNSW's accuracy. Many systems combine IVF with product quantization to shrink memory further.
When would product quantization be worth the accuracy loss?

Product quantization splits each vector into subvectors and replaces each subvector with the index of its nearest centroid in a small codebook, so a 768-dimension float32 vector of 3,072 bytes can compress to roughly 64 bytes. It is worth the accuracy loss when the dataset is too large to hold in RAM at full precision, when memory cost dominates the budget, or when approximate distances are acceptable for a first-stage candidate pool. A common pattern is to retrieve a larger set with compressed codes and then rerank the top candidates using full-precision vectors, which recovers much of the lost recall. Choosing the number of subvectors and bits per code is a tradeoff between compression ratio and distortion, so it should be validated against a recall benchmark on representative queries.
What should I look for when evaluating how well a vector database handles filtered queries?

Filtered search, where a similarity query must also match metadata conditions, is a common source of problems. Key things to check include whether filtering happens before, during, or after the ANN search. Post-filtering can return fewer results than requested when the filter is selective, while pre-filtering can break graph traversal and hurt recall or latency. Good systems use filter-aware traversal or adaptive strategies that switch based on estimated selectivity. Evaluate recall and p95 latency at several selectivity levels, for example filters that keep 90 percent, 10 percent, and 0.1 percent of records, and test under concurrent writes, since index updates can degrade filtered performance over time.
How does BM25 ranking work?

BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function that scores a document against a query by summing a score for each query term. For each term, it combines two factors. The first is inverse document frequency, which gives rare terms more weight than common ones, usually computed as log((N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)), where N is the number of documents and n is the number of documents containing the term. The second is a term frequency component that saturates: it rises with the term's count in the document but levels off, controlled by a parameter k1, typically around 1.2 to 2.0. The score is also normalized for document length relative to the average length, using a parameter b, usually set near 0.75. Setting b to 0 ignores length, while b equal to 1 fully normalizes by it.
What's the difference between the k1 and b parameters in practice?

k1 controls how quickly repeated occurrences of a term stop helping. A low k1 makes the score saturate fast, so the tenth occurrence adds little beyond the second or third. A high k1 keeps rewarding repetition for longer, approaching a raw term-count behavior. The b parameter controls length normalization. With b at 0, a long document gets no penalty for being long, so it can win simply by containing more text. With b at 1, term frequency is scaled fully by the ratio of document length to average length, so long documents are penalized heavily. Values around 0.75 for b and 1.2 to 1.5 for k1 are common defaults, but the best settings depend on the collection and are usually tuned on relevance judgments.
Why is the saturation behavior useful compared with plain term counts?

Plain term counts assume that each additional occurrence of a word adds the same amount of evidence that the document is relevant. In practice, the first few occurrences carry most of the signal, and later ones add diminishing information. A document that mentions a term fifty times is not usually fifty times more about the query than one that mentions it five times. Saturation prevents keyword-stuffed or very repetitive documents from dominating results. It also makes scores more stable across documents of different lengths, since the contribution of any single term is bounded. The bound is roughly (k1 + 1) times the IDF, so no single term can overwhelm the others in a multi-term query.

topic: hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion

turns.text: What is hybrid search and why do people combine keyword and vector retrieval?

Hybrid search runs two retrieval methods over the same corpus and merges their results. Keyword retrieval, usually BM25 over an inverted index, excels at exact matches such as product codes, error messages, and rare names, because it scores documents by term frequency and inverse document frequency. Vector retrieval embeds queries and documents into a dense space and ranks by similarity, so it handles paraphrases and synonyms well, for example matching "car repair" to a document about "automobile maintenance." Each method fails in ways the other covers. Combining them usually improves recall across both exact and semantic queries. The hard part is that the two scoring systems produce scores on incompatible scales, which is why the merge step needs a method that does not depend on raw score values.
So how does reciprocal rank fusion handle that scale problem?

Reciprocal rank fusion, or RRF, ignores the raw scores entirely and uses only each document's rank in each result list. For every list where a document appears, it adds 1 divided by (k + rank) to that document's total, where rank is 1-based and k is a constant, commonly 60. A document ranked first in both lists gets 2/61, about 0.0328. A document ranked first in one list and tenth in the other gets 1/61 plus 1/70. Because the contributions depend only on position, BM25 scores and cosine similarities never need normalizing against each other. The constant k dampens the advantage of top positions, so a document consistently ranked fairly well across lists can outrank one that is first in only a single list.
Why is k set to 60, and does changing it matter much?

The value 60 comes from the original RRF paper by Cormack, Clarke, and Büttcher in 2009, where it was chosen empirically and found to work robustly across several TREC collections without tuning. Its effect is on how steeply contributions fall off with rank. With a small k, such as 1, the first-ranked item dominates: 1/2 versus 1/3 for second place is a large gap. With a large k, the curve flattens, so ranks deep in the list still contribute meaningfully and agreement across lists matters more than being first in one. In practice, the choice is rarely critical within a moderate range, and 60 is a sensible default. If a system needs tuning, it is usually easier to adjust per-retriever weights than to change k, since weights let one retriever count more heavily than the other.
What are the main drawbacks of RRF compared with a learned score-combination approach?

The main drawback is that RRF discards score magnitude. If the top BM25 result has a score far above the rest, indicating a very confident exact match, RRF treats it the same as a top result with a marginal score. A learned approach, such as a weighted linear combination of normalized scores or a learned reranker, can exploit that confidence information, but it needs labeled relevance data to fit its weights and must be recalibrated when the corpus or embedding model changes. RRF needs no training and is robust to score distribution shifts, which is why it is a common default in production systems like Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Many teams start with RRF and move to score-based fusion or a cross-encoder reranker only when they have enough evaluation data to justify the extra complexity.
How does a cross-encoder reranker work, and how is it different from a bi-encoder?

A cross-encoder takes a query and a candidate document as a single concatenated input, typically separated by a special token such as [SEP] in BERT-style models. The transformer applies full self-attention across both sequences, so every query token can attend to every document token. A classification or regression head on the final representation, often the [CLS] token, outputs a relevance score. A bi-encoder, by contrast, encodes the query and the document independently into fixed vectors, and relevance is computed afterward with a cheap similarity function like dot product or cosine. Because document vectors can be precomputed and indexed, bi-encoders scale to millions of documents. Cross-encoders are more accurate because they model fine-grained interactions between query and document, but they must run a forward pass for every query-document pair, which is why they are usually used to rerank a short candidate list.
Why is the cost so high in practice, and how do systems usually deal with that?

The cost comes from the quadratic attention over the joint sequence and from the fact that nothing can be cached: each query-document pair requires a fresh forward pass through the full model. If you have a query and 1,000 candidates of 256 tokens each, that is 1,000 transformer inferences per query. Common mitigations include a two-stage pipeline, where a fast first-stage retriever such as BM25 or a bi-encoder returns the top 50 to 200 candidates and the cross-encoder reranks only those. Teams also use smaller distilled models like MiniLM variants, truncate documents to the first few hundred tokens, batch pairs on GPUs, and apply early stopping or dynamic pruning. Some systems use late-interaction models such as ColBERT as a middle ground, since they keep token-level precomputed representations while still allowing finer matching than a single vector.
When would someone choose to skip the reranker entirely?

A reranker is worth skipping when latency or throughput budgets are very tight, when the first-stage retriever already performs well on the task, or when the corpus is small enough that exact search is cheap. Reranking also adds little when candidates are nearly identical in relevance, since the model cannot separate them meaningfully. Another case is when the query distribution is dominated by exact-match lookups, such as product codes or identifiers, where lexical methods like BM25 are already precise and a neural reranker may even demote correct results. Evaluation should guide the decision: measure nDCG or MRR at the reranked depth with and without the cross-encoder, and compare against the added p95 latency and serving cost. If the gain is marginal, a cheaper approach such as query expansion or hybrid lexical-plus-dense retrieval may deliver better value.
What are the main chunking strategies used in RAG pipelines?

The most common chunking strategies are fixed-size chunking, where text is split into windows of a set number of tokens or characters, often with overlap; recursive character splitting, which tries progressively finer separators such as paragraphs, then sentences, then words until chunks fit a size limit; structure-aware chunking, which follows document boundaries like headings, HTML tags, or code blocks; semantic chunking, which groups consecutive sentences based on embedding similarity so that topic shifts mark boundaries; and agentic or LLM-based chunking, where a model proposes split points. Fixed-size is simplest and cheapest, while semantic and structure-aware methods usually preserve meaning better at the cost of more processing.
How does overlap between chunks help, and how much overlap is typical?

Overlap repeats a portion of the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so that a sentence or idea spanning a boundary is still fully contained in at least one chunk. Without overlap, a key fact split across two chunks may never match a query strongly enough to be retrieved. Common settings are 10 to 20 percent of the chunk size, for example 50 to 100 tokens for 512-token chunks. Too much overlap inflates the index with redundant vectors and can crowd out diverse results at retrieval time, so the value is usually tuned against retrieval metrics on a sample of real queries.
Given that, how should chunk size be chosen relative to the embedding model and the LLM context?

Three constraints matter. First, the embedding model has a maximum input length, and text beyond it is silently truncated, so chunks must fit within that limit. Second, smaller chunks produce more precise embeddings that match specific questions, while larger chunks carry more context but dilute the vector's meaning. Third, the total retrieved text, multiplied by the number of chunks returned, must fit comfortably in the LLM's context window alongside the prompt and the answer. A practical approach is to start with a moderate size such as 256 to 512 tokens, retrieve the top k chunks, and then adjust size and k based on answer quality and latency.
What are some ways to keep context when chunks are small, besides overlap?

A widely used technique is parent-child or small-to-big retrieval: documents are indexed as small chunks for precise matching, but each chunk stores a reference to its larger parent section, and the parent is passed to the LLM. Another is adding contextual headers, where each chunk is prefixed with its document title and section path so the embedding and the generator know where it came from. Some pipelines also generate a short LLM summary of the surrounding document and prepend it to each chunk before embedding, as in contextual retrieval approaches. Metadata such as page number, author, or date can be stored alongside chunks and used for filtering or re-ranking.
How do you evaluate a retrieval-augmented generation system? What are the main things to measure?

RAG evaluation is usually split into two parts: the retriever and the generator. For retrieval, the standard metrics are recall@k (whether the relevant documents appear in the top k results), precision@k, and mean reciprocal rank or normalized discounted cumulative gain when ranking order matters. These require a labeled set of queries paired with relevant chunks. For generation, you typically measure faithfulness (whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context), answer relevance (whether the answer addresses the question), and correctness against a reference answer when one exists. Context relevance, which asks whether the retrieved passages are actually useful for the question, sits between the two and helps diagnose which component is failing. Frameworks such as RAGAS formalize several of these metrics, often using an LLM as a judge.
You mentioned using an LLM as a judge. How reliable is that approach, and how would you check it?

LLM-as-a-judge is useful for scaling evaluation, but it has known weaknesses: position bias in pairwise comparisons, verbosity bias that favors longer answers, self-preference when the judge is the same model family as the generator, and sensitivity to prompt wording. To check reliability, first run a small human-labeled set, often a few hundred examples, and compute agreement with the judge using Cohen's kappa or simple accuracy. Then test robustness by shuffling answer order, paraphrasing the judge prompt, and comparing scores across judge models. Calibration also matters: if the judge gives binary faithfulness labels, check its false positive rate on deliberately corrupted answers. Re-running this audit whenever the judge model or prompt changes keeps the metric trustworthy over time.
Once those checks pass, how would you set up a regression test so changes to the pipeline don't quietly degrade quality?

A practical approach is to maintain a versioned evaluation set of representative queries, ideally including known hard cases, edge cases, and questions with no answer in the corpus. Each pipeline change, such as a new embedding model, chunk size, reranker, or prompt, runs against this set automatically in continuous integration. Store the retrieved contexts, generated answers, and metric scores for every run so results can be compared against a baseline. Set thresholds per metric and fail the build when a score drops beyond a tolerance, using confidence intervals or repeated runs to separate real regressions from sampling noise. Review a random sample of outputs manually each cycle, since automated metrics can miss issues like tone or formatting. Finally, track latency and cost alongside quality, because a change that improves answers but doubles response time may still be a regression.
What is chain-of-thought prompting and how does it work?

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting asks a language model to show intermediate reasoning steps before giving a final answer. Instead of asking for only the result of a multi-step math word problem, the prompt includes examples or an instruction such as "think step by step," which leads the model to decompose the problem into smaller parts. Because each generated step conditions the next token predictions, the model can use earlier intermediate results to reach a conclusion. CoT tends to help most on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks, and it works best with larger models. It can also make outputs easier to inspect, since the reasoning is visible and errors can be traced to a specific step.
How is that different from few-shot prompting, and can the two be combined?

Few-shot prompting includes several input-output examples in the prompt so the model infers the task format and pattern, while the answers themselves are just labels or final results. Chain-of-thought focuses on the content of the reasoning: each example includes the worked steps that lead to the answer. The two are commonly combined. A few-shot CoT prompt provides examples where the reasoning is written out, and the model imitates that structure on a new question. This often outperforms plain few-shot prompting on tasks requiring multi-step logic. Example selection matters, though: examples should be representative of the target problems, correctly solved, and formatted consistently so the model can reliably copy the pattern.
What are some common pitfalls when writing prompts with examples like that?

Several pitfalls come up often. First, label imbalance: if most examples share one answer, the model may bias toward that label. Second, ordering effects: the same examples in a different order can change results, so testing several orderings helps. Third, format drift: inconsistent delimiters or phrasing between examples makes the pattern harder to copy. Fourth, overly similar examples can cause the model to overfit to surface features rather than the underlying task. Fifth, errors in the examples themselves get imitated, especially in reasoning chains. Finally, long example sets consume context window space and can increase cost. Evaluating prompts on a held-out set of inputs, rather than judging by a few hand-picked cases, is the most reliable way to catch these issues.
Given those pitfalls, how would you go about systematically evaluating a prompt before deploying it?

A systematic evaluation usually follows a few steps. Begin by defining the success criteria, such as exact-match accuracy, rubric scores, or format compliance. Next, assemble a labeled dataset that reflects real inputs, including edge cases and examples the prompt was not tuned on, and split it so that prompt development and final testing use different data. Run each prompt variant across the dataset with fixed settings like temperature, and record outputs. Compare variants using the defined metrics, and check the failure cases manually to see whether errors cluster around a specific category. Test sensitivity by shuffling example order and paraphrasing instructions. Finally, monitor the prompt after deployment with sampled outputs, since model updates and shifting input distributions can change behavior over time.
What's the difference between few-shot and zero-shot prompting?

Zero-shot prompting asks a language model to perform a task using only an instruction, with no examples of the desired input-output behavior. For instance, you might write "Classify this review as positive or negative: The battery died within an hour." Few-shot prompting includes a small number of worked examples in the prompt before the actual query, such as two or three review-label pairs. The examples show the model the expected format, labeling conventions, and level of detail. Few-shot tends to improve consistency and accuracy on tasks with ambiguous or unusual output formats, while zero-shot is faster to write and uses fewer tokens.
When would zero-shot actually be good enough?

Zero-shot usually works well when the task is common and the model has likely seen many similar instances during training. Examples include general summarization, translation between major languages, answering factual questions, or simple sentiment classification with clear categories. It also suits cases where the instruction can be stated precisely and the output format is obvious. If results are already accurate and consistent, adding examples only increases prompt length and cost. A practical approach is to start with zero-shot, inspect failures, and add examples only when specific error patterns appear, such as wrong label names, verbose outputs, or misread edge cases.
How do you choose which examples to include in a few-shot prompt?

Good examples should be representative of the real inputs the model will see, including typical cases and a few difficult or boundary cases. Diversity matters: cover each label or output category, and vary the length and phrasing so the model does not learn spurious patterns, such as always associating a label with a particular word. Ordering can also affect results, so it helps to avoid placing all examples of one class together and to test a few orderings. Keep the examples consistent in format with the target query. Finally, evaluate on a held-out set rather than the examples themselves, since performance on the prompt's own examples can overstate how well the approach generalizes.
How does temperature actually change the output of a language model?

Temperature rescales the logits before the softmax. The model produces a raw score for every token in its vocabulary, and each score is divided by the temperature T before being converted into probabilities. When T is below 1, the differences between scores are amplified, so the highest-scoring tokens dominate and the distribution becomes sharper. When T is above 1, the differences shrink, so lower-ranked tokens get a larger share of probability and the output becomes more varied and less predictable. As T approaches 0, sampling approaches greedy decoding, which always picks the single most likely token. Temperature does not change what the model knows; it only changes how strictly the model follows its own probability estimates when choosing each next token.
What's the difference between top-k and top-p sampling, and how do they relate to temperature?

Both methods truncate the candidate pool before sampling. Top-k keeps only the k tokens with the highest probabilities and renormalizes among them, so the pool size is fixed regardless of how the distribution looks. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, so the pool adapts: it is small when the model is confident and large when many continuations are plausible. Temperature is applied first, which reshapes the distribution, and then the truncation is applied to the reshaped distribution. A low temperature makes the top-p nucleus contain fewer tokens, while a high temperature spreads probability out and enlarges it. In practice, many people combine a moderate temperature with top-p rather than using either one alone.
Why do models sometimes repeat themselves when temperature is set very low?

Low temperature makes the model consistently choose the highest-probability token, and high-probability continuations are often generic or self-reinforcing. Once a phrase appears, the model's context contains it, which can make repeating it even more probable at the next step. This creates loops where a sentence or paragraph is reproduced over and over. Greedy or near-greedy decoding is especially prone to this because it never explores alternatives that would break the cycle. Common mitigations include a modest temperature above zero, a repetition penalty that lowers the score of tokens already present in the context, or n-gram blocking that forbids exact repeats of a given length. Choosing a value usually involves balancing coherence against variety, and the best setting depends on the task.
Is there a standard range of temperature values that people use for different tasks?

There is no universal standard, but common practice follows rough patterns. For tasks with a single correct answer, such as arithmetic, classification, or extracting a field from text, temperatures near 0 to 0.2 are typical because they favor consistency. For general question answering and summarization, values around 0.3 to 0.7 are common, giving accurate but natural phrasing. For brainstorming, creative writing, or generating diverse candidates, values near 0.8 to 1.0 are often used, and some practitioners go higher. Values above about 1.2 tend to produce incoherent text in many models. Because each model's logit scale differs, these ranges are approximate, and the best approach is to test a few settings on representative inputs and measure the results.

topic: LLM context windows and long context

turns.text: What does the context window mean for a large language model?

The context window is the maximum number of tokens a language model can process in a single forward pass, counting both the input prompt and the text it generates. Tokens are sub-word units, so a window of 8,000 tokens holds roughly 6,000 English words. The model has no persistent memory beyond this window; anything outside it, such as earlier messages in a long conversation, is simply not visible to the model when it produces the next token. Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length in standard transformers, which is one reason window sizes were historically small. Modern models have expanded these limits considerably, with some supporting hundreds of thousands or even over a million tokens.
If context windows have grown so much, why do long inputs still cause problems?

Several issues persist even when a model accepts a long input. The best-known is the lost-in-the-middle effect: models tend to retrieve information more reliably from the beginning and end of the context than from the middle, so accuracy can drop when a relevant passage is buried in the center. Latency and cost also rise with input length, since the prompt must be processed on every request unless it is cached. Additionally, more irrelevant text can dilute the model's attention and increase the chance of it being distracted by superficially similar content. Benchmarks that measure performance at the full advertised length often show weaker results than short-context tests suggest, so the usable window can be smaller than the nominal one.
What techniques are used to get around these limits in practice?

A common approach is retrieval-augmented generation, where documents are split into chunks, embedded as vectors, and only the most relevant chunks are inserted into the prompt for a given query. This keeps the input short and focused. Another technique is summarization or rolling memory, where older conversation turns are condensed into a summary that replaces the raw text. Prompt caching reduces cost when a large shared prefix, such as a codebase or manual, is reused across many requests. On the model side, methods like rotary position embedding scaling and continued training on longer sequences extend the window, while sparse or linear attention variants reduce the quadratic compute cost. In practice, many systems combine these methods rather than relying on a single one.
What does it mean when an LLM hallucinates?

When a large language model hallucinates, it generates output that is fluent and confident but factually wrong, unsupported by its training data or by any provided source. Because these models are trained to predict the most likely next token given the preceding text, they optimize for plausibility rather than verified truth. A hallucination can take many forms: an invented citation with a real-looking author and journal, a fabricated historical date, a nonexistent software library function, or a made-up quotation attributed to a real person. The model does not have an internal fact-checking step by default, so it may present these errors with the same tone it uses for correct statements. Hallucinations are a central reliability problem because users often cannot tell the difference without independent verification.
What causes them in the first place?

Several factors contribute. First, training data is noisy and incomplete, so the model learns patterns that include errors, contradictions, and gaps. Second, the next-token objective rewards producing a continuation that sounds right, even when the model lacks the underlying knowledge; when it is uncertain, it often fills the gap with a plausible guess. Third, rare facts appear few times in training, so the model's representation of them is weak and easily confused with similar entities. Fourth, decoding settings such as high sampling temperature increase the chance of low-probability, incorrect tokens. Finally, the model has no direct access to a verified database at inference time, so it relies on compressed statistical memory. Research also suggests that post-training that rewards confident answers over admissions of uncertainty can encourage guessing.
So how do developers reduce hallucinations in practice?

A common approach is retrieval-augmented generation, where the system fetches relevant documents from a trusted source and instructs the model to answer only from that context, ideally with citations. Developers also use tool calls, such as code execution, calculators, or search APIs, so that factual or numerical claims are computed or looked up rather than recalled. Lowering the sampling temperature makes outputs more deterministic. Fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback can teach the model to say when it does not know something. Evaluation matters too: teams build test sets with known answers and measure faithfulness against source documents. Finally, automated checks, such as verifying that quoted text appears in the source or that cited URLs resolve, catch some errors before they reach users. No single technique eliminates hallucinations, so layered defenses are typically used.
Which of those methods works best for the citation problem specifically?

For fabricated citations, retrieval-augmented generation combined with programmatic verification is usually the most effective. The model is given a set of retrieved documents with identifiers, and it is constrained to cite only those identifiers. A post-processing step then checks each citation against the source index, confirming that the DOI, title, or URL exists and that the quoted passage actually appears in the document. Citations that fail the check are removed or flagged. Asking the model to generate references from memory is the riskiest pattern, since it will often produce plausible but nonexistent papers. Reference lookup through bibliographic databases such as Crossref can add a further layer. The key principle is that the model should point to sources it was given, and software should verify those pointers rather than trusting the model's own claims.
How does function calling work in LLM APIs?

Function calling lets a developer describe tools to the model using a JSON Schema for each function's name, description, and parameters. When the model receives a prompt along with these definitions, it can decide that a tool is needed and, instead of plain text, return a structured call containing the function name and arguments as JSON. The application then parses that output, runs the actual function in its own code, and sends the result back to the model as a new message with a tool role. The model uses that result to compose its final response. The model never executes code itself; it only proposes calls, and the surrounding application remains responsible for running them and validating inputs.
What's the difference between that and just asking the model to output JSON?

The main difference is how the output is constrained and routed. Asking for JSON in a prompt is a best-effort request, so the model may add commentary, miss fields, or malformed syntax. Function calling is a dedicated API feature: the tool schema is provided separately, the provider is trained to emit well-formed arguments matching that schema, and the response is typically marked as a tool call rather than ordinary text. This makes parsing more reliable and lets the model choose among several tools. Some providers also offer structured outputs, which enforce a schema on the response itself, but function calling additionally handles the loop of calling external actions and returning their results.
How should an application handle it when the model calls a function with bad arguments?

Treat the model's arguments as untrusted input. First, validate them against the same JSON Schema you supplied, checking types, required fields, and allowed enum values. If validation fails, you can return an error message as the tool result, describing which field was wrong, and let the model retry with corrected arguments. Limit the number of retries to avoid loops. For destructive or sensitive actions, require explicit user confirmation before execution. Also enforce authorization inside the function itself rather than trusting the model's choice, and log each call and result for auditing. Keeping tool descriptions precise and parameter counts small also reduces the chance of malformed calls in the first place.
How does structured output with a JSON schema work when calling a language model?

Structured outputs constrain a model's generation so that its response always conforms to a supplied JSON Schema. The schema defines the allowed object shapes, property names, types, and required fields. During decoding, the inference engine masks out tokens that would violate the schema at the current position, so the output is guaranteed to parse and validate. Unlike plain JSON mode, which only ensures syntactically valid JSON, schema-constrained decoding also enforces the specific keys and value types. In practice you pass the schema in the request, often alongside a description of the task, and the response arrives as a JSON string that your code can parse directly without retries or regex-based cleanup.
What's the difference between JSON mode and a JSON schema constraint?

JSON mode guarantees only that the output is valid JSON, so the model may invent any keys, omit fields you expected, or return values of the wrong type. A JSON schema constraint goes further by fixing the structure. You specify the properties, their types, enums, nested objects, and which fields are required, and the decoder will only produce tokens consistent with that definition. A typical difference shows up in extraction tasks. With JSON mode you might get a date as "March 3" in one response and "2024-03-03" in another. With a schema declaring a string with format date, or an enum of allowed categories, the values follow one pattern every time. The tradeoff is that complex schemas can add latency on first use and may restrict some JSON Schema keywords.
Which JSON Schema features are usually supported in these constrained decoders?

Support varies by provider, but most implementations handle the core vocabulary: object with properties and required, arrays with items, string, number, integer, boolean, and null types, plus enum and const. Many also support nested objects and anyOf for union types. Some keywords are often unsupported or limited, such as numeric bounds like minimum and maximum, string length constraints, uniqueItems, and certain pattern regexes, or they may be ignored and checked only in client-side validation. Recursive schemas using $ref are supported by some engines but not others. The practical approach is to check your provider's documentation, keep schemas relatively flat, set additionalProperties to false on objects so the model cannot add unexpected keys, and validate the result on your side anyway as a safeguard.
How should I handle cases where the model can't produce a valid answer for my schema?

A common pattern is to add an explicit fallback to the schema. You can include a boolean or enum field such as refused or status, or a nullable field for the answer, so the model has a legitimate way to signal that the input does not contain the requested information. Without such an escape hatch, a constrained decoder may be forced to fill required fields with plausible but fabricated values. Your application should then check that flag before reading the data. It also helps to keep the schema minimal, provide clear descriptions for each property, and log responses where the flag is set so you can refine the prompt or schema. For any output that feeds a downstream system, combine the schema constraint with server-side validation and a retry or error path for the rare cases where the request is rejected or truncated by token limits.
What are the main design patterns used when building AI agents?

Several patterns recur across agent systems. ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions: the model writes a thought, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until it can answer. Plan-and-execute separates planning from acting: a planner produces a multi-step plan up front, and an executor carries out each step, which makes costs and progress easier to track. Reflection adds a critique loop in which the model reviews its own output and revises it. Multi-agent orchestration assigns roles to specialized agents coordinated by a supervisor or passed through a fixed workflow. Finally, tool use, where the model emits structured function calls that a runtime executes, underlies most of the others.
How does the reflection pattern work in practice, and when does it help more than it costs?

In practice, reflection runs a generate-critique-revise cycle. The agent produces a draft, then a second prompt, often with the same model, asks it to check the draft against explicit criteria such as factual claims, missing requirements, or code that fails tests. The critique is fed back with the draft, and the loop repeats until the critic finds no issues or a round limit is hit. It helps most when there is an objective check available, such as unit tests, a compiler, or a retrieval source, because the critic can ground its feedback. Without such signals, the model often rubber-stamps its own output while doubling or tripling token cost and latency. A common safeguard is to cap iterations and stop early when a verifier passes.
How would plan-and-execute compare with ReAct when a task has many dependent steps?

With many dependent steps, plan-and-execute usually has the advantage in structure, while ReAct has the advantage in adaptability. A plan-and-execute agent drafts the full sequence first, so the dependencies are explicit and independent steps can run in parallel. It also uses a stronger model for planning and cheaper models for execution. The weakness is brittleness: if step two returns unexpected data, the original plan may be stale. ReAct decides one action at a time, so it reacts to every observation, but it can wander, repeat tool calls, or lose track of the overall goal over long horizons. A hybrid is common: create a plan, execute steps via a ReAct loop, and replan when a step fails or its output contradicts the plan.
How does LangGraph model a workflow as a state machine?

LangGraph represents a workflow as a directed graph. You define a shared state schema, typically a TypedDict or Pydantic model, that holds the data passed between steps. Each node is a Python function that receives the current state and returns a partial update, which LangGraph merges into the state using reducers. Edges define which node runs next. Normal edges are fixed transitions, while conditional edges call a routing function that inspects the state and returns the name of the next node. Execution starts at a designated entry point and continues until it reaches the special END node. Because each step reads and writes a well-defined state, the graph behaves like a state machine where the state is the memory and the nodes are the transitions' actions.
What's the difference between a normal edge and a conditional edge in practice?

A normal edge always routes from one node to a specific next node, so the path is fixed at build time. A conditional edge is attached to a routing function that runs after the source node finishes. The function reads the current state and returns a key, and a mapping dictionary translates that key to a destination node. For example, a classifier node might set a field called category to either billing or technical, and a conditional edge would send billing requests to one node and technical requests to another. You can also omit the mapping and have the function return node names directly. Conditional edges are what make loops and branching possible, such as retrying a generation step until a validation node marks the output as acceptable.
How do reducers affect how state updates get merged when several nodes write to the same key?

By default, a key in the state has no reducer, so a later write simply overwrites the earlier value. When a key is annotated with a reducer, such as Annotated[list, operator.add], LangGraph calls that function to combine the old value with the new one. With operator.add, lists returned by different nodes are concatenated, which is useful for accumulating messages or logs. If several nodes run in the same superstep, which happens with parallel fan-out, their updates are applied through the reducer in a deterministic order, so the reducer must be associative enough for that to make sense. Custom reducers can implement policies like keeping the maximum score or deduplicating items. The LangGraph messages reducer is a specialized version that appends new messages and also updates existing ones when their IDs match.
Can you show how checkpointing fits in with this, for example to pause a graph for human review?

Checkpointing saves a snapshot of the state after each superstep, keyed by a thread ID. To use it, you compile the graph with a checkpointer such as MemorySaver for testing or a database-backed saver for production, for example graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=saver). To pause for human review, you can compile with interrupt_before=["approve"] or call interrupt() inside a node. The run stops and returns control to the caller. You then inspect the saved state, optionally modify it with update_state, and resume by invoking the graph with None as input and the same config containing the thread ID. Because the state lives in the checkpoint rather than in process memory, the pause can last minutes or days, and the workflow resumes from exactly the saved point.

topic: model quantization: GPTQ vs AWQ vs GGUF

turns.text: What's the difference between GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF for quantizing language models?

They are different formats and methods that target different runtimes. GPTQ is a post-training quantization method that uses approximate second-order information (based on the Hessian) to adjust weights layer by layer, typically to 4-bit or 3-bit, and is commonly run on GPU with libraries like AutoGPTQ or ExLlama kernels. AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) instead identifies the small fraction of weight channels that matter most by looking at activation magnitudes, scales those channels before rounding, and preserves them better at 4-bit, often with faster inference in GPU serving stacks such as vLLM. GGUF is not a quantization algorithm but a file format used by llama.cpp; it packages quantized weights in types like Q4_K_M or Q5_K_S and runs efficiently on CPUs, Apple Silicon, and mixed CPU/GPU setups.
Given that, when would GGUF be a better choice than GPTQ or AWQ?

GGUF is usually the better choice when you need flexible hardware support or partial offloading. Because llama.cpp can split layers between system RAM and GPU VRAM, a model too large for the GPU can still run, just more slowly. It also performs well on CPUs and Apple Silicon, where GPTQ and AWQ kernels are often unavailable or poorly optimized. GGUF offers many quantization levels, including k-quant variants that mix precisions across tensors, so you can trade size against quality in finer steps. GPTQ and AWQ tend to win when the whole model fits in GPU memory and you need high batched throughput on a server, since their CUDA kernels and integrations with serving frameworks are built for that scenario.
How much quality loss should I expect at 4-bit with each of these methods?

At 4-bit, all three methods usually keep most of the model's quality, but the exact loss depends on the model and the benchmark. On perplexity tests for Llama-family models of 7B and larger, AWQ and GPTQ with group size 128 typically add a small increase in perplexity, often under about 0.1 to 0.3 points relative to fp16, and AWQ often edges out GPTQ on instruction-following tasks. GGUF k-quants such as Q4_K_M are similarly close, and the medium variant often matches or beats basic 4-bit GPTQ because it keeps sensitive tensors at higher precision. Smaller models, under about 3B parameters, degrade more noticeably at 4-bit, so testing on your own evaluation set is worthwhile before choosing a format.
How does LoRA work for fine-tuning large language models?

LoRA, or Low-Rank Adaptation, freezes the pretrained weights of a model and injects small trainable matrices alongside selected layers, usually the attention projections. For a weight matrix W of shape d by k, LoRA represents the update as the product of two smaller matrices, B of shape d by r and A of shape r by k, where the rank r is typically between 4 and 64. The forward pass computes Wx plus BAx, scaled by alpha divided by r. B is initialized to zero so training starts from the original model's behavior. Because only A and B receive gradients, the number of trainable parameters often drops to well under one percent of the full model, which greatly reduces memory and storage needs for each task-specific adapter.
What's the difference between LoRA and QLoRA?

QLoRA builds on LoRA but adds quantization to reduce the memory footprint of the frozen base model. In standard LoRA, the base weights stay in 16-bit precision. QLoRA loads the base model in 4-bit precision using a data type called NF4, which is designed for normally distributed weights, and it uses double quantization to also compress the quantization constants. During the forward and backward passes, the 4-bit weights are dequantized to bfloat16 for computation, while the LoRA adapter weights remain in higher precision and are the only parameters updated. The result is that very large models, such as those with 65 billion parameters, can be fine-tuned on a single 48 GB GPU, with quality close to full 16-bit LoRA in reported benchmarks.
What is paged optimizer memory in QLoRA, and why is it needed?

Paged optimizers are a second memory-saving feature in QLoRA, and they address memory spikes rather than the steady-state model size. Optimizer states, such as the first and second moments in Adam, can grow large, and sudden spikes can occur when processing long sequences or batches with big gradients, causing out-of-memory errors. QLoRA uses NVIDIA unified memory so that optimizer states can be automatically paged between GPU memory and CPU RAM, similar to virtual memory in an operating system. When GPU memory runs short during a spike, pages are evicted to CPU memory and loaded back when needed. This keeps training stable on consumer or limited hardware, at the cost of some throughput when paging occurs.
When would someone choose plain LoRA over QLoRA?

Plain LoRA is generally preferred when enough GPU memory is available to hold the base model in 16-bit precision, since it avoids the computational overhead of dequantizing 4-bit weights on every forward and backward pass. This typically makes training faster and can give slightly better numerical fidelity. QLoRA is the better choice when memory is the main constraint, for example when fine-tuning a large model on a single GPU or a modest cluster. Another consideration is the deployment path: adapters trained with QLoRA can be merged into a higher-precision base model afterward, so the memory savings during training do not necessarily carry into inference. Practitioners usually benchmark both approaches on their target task to see whether the quality difference matters.
What is RLHF and how does it work at a high level?

RLHF stands for reinforcement learning from human feedback. It is a training method used to align language models with human preferences beyond what raw next-token prediction provides. The process typically has three stages. First, a pretrained model is fine-tuned on demonstrations of desired behavior, often written by human labelers. Second, human raters compare pairs of model outputs for the same prompt, and those comparisons are used to train a reward model that predicts which response people would prefer. Third, the language model is optimized with a reinforcement learning algorithm, commonly PPO, to produce responses that score highly under the reward model, usually with a penalty that keeps it close to the original model.
Why is a separate reward model needed instead of having humans rate every output directly?

Direct human rating during training would be too slow and expensive, since reinforcement learning needs enormous numbers of model outputs scored in a loop. The reward model solves this by learning a compressed approximation of human judgment from a comparatively small set of pairwise preferences. Once trained, it can score millions of candidate responses automatically. Pairwise comparisons are used rather than absolute ratings because people are more consistent when asked which of two answers is better than when asked to assign a numeric score. The tradeoff is that the reward model is only an approximation, so the policy can learn to exploit its blind spots, a failure mode known as reward hacking, which is why the KL penalty and ongoing evaluation are important.
What's the difference between DPO and PPO for aligning language models?

PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm used in RLHF. It requires first training a reward model on human preference data, then optimizing the language model policy against that reward with a clipped surrogate objective, usually with a KL penalty to a reference model. It also typically needs a value function (critic), so training involves four models: the policy, the reference, the reward model, and the critic. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) skips the explicit reward model and the RL loop. It reformulates the RLHF objective so the policy is trained directly on preference pairs (chosen vs. rejected responses) with a simple classification-style loss that implicitly measures the reward as a log-ratio against the reference model. This makes DPO simpler and more stable to train, though PPO can be more flexible with online sampling and arbitrary reward signals.
Why does DPO's implicit reward come from a log-ratio against the reference model?

The derivation starts from the standard KL-regularized RLHF objective, whose optimal policy has a closed form: the reference policy reweighted by the exponentiated reward, divided by a partition function. Rearranging that expression gives the reward as beta times the log of the ratio between the optimal policy and the reference policy, plus a term depending only on the prompt. Because the partition term cancels when you compare two responses to the same prompt in a Bradley-Terry preference model, the preference probability depends only on the difference of these log-ratios. DPO substitutes the policy itself for the optimal policy and maximizes the likelihood of the observed preferences. The beta parameter controls how far the policy may drift from the reference, playing the same role as the KL coefficient in PPO.
So what are the practical trade-offs when choosing between them?

DPO is cheaper and easier to implement: it needs only the policy and a frozen reference model, runs like supervised fine-tuning on a fixed preference dataset, and avoids reward model training and the sensitivity of RL hyperparameters. PPO is more expensive, since it holds four models in memory and requires generating fresh samples during training, but it can exploit on-policy data, which helps when the model's outputs drift away from the original dataset. It also works with any scalar reward, including verifiable rewards like unit test passes or math answer correctness. DPO can overfit preference pairs, sometimes lowering the likelihood of chosen responses too, and it may struggle with long-horizon or multi-step credit assignment. Many teams start with DPO for speed and move to PPO-style or online methods when they need stronger performance on hard objectives.
Are there variants that try to combine the strengths of both?

Yes. Iterative or online DPO generates new responses from the current policy, scores them with a reward model or a judge, and builds fresh preference pairs each round, bringing some on-policy benefits while keeping the DPO loss. IPO (Identity Preference Optimization) modifies the loss to avoid overfitting when preferences are near-deterministic. KTO uses unpaired thumbs-up and thumbs-down labels instead of pairs. SimPO removes the reference model and uses length-normalized log-likelihood as the implicit reward, cutting memory use further. On the PPO side, GRPO drops the learned critic and estimates advantages from a group of sampled responses to the same prompt, reducing memory cost while keeping online RL updates. These methods reflect a general trend of trading some of PPO's flexibility for simpler, cheaper training.
What is knowledge distillation in machine learning, and how does it work?

Knowledge distillation is a technique for transferring what a large, high-performing model has learned into a smaller, cheaper model. The large model is called the teacher and the small one is the student. Instead of training the student only on hard labels such as "cat" or "dog," the student is trained to match the teacher's output probabilities, often called soft targets. These soft targets carry information about how the teacher ranks the wrong classes too, for example that a cat image looks more like a dog than a truck. A temperature parameter is usually applied to the softmax to smooth these distributions, and the student's loss combines a term for matching the teacher with the standard cross-entropy loss on the true labels. The result is typically a compact model that retains much of the teacher's accuracy at a fraction of the compute and memory cost.
Why would soft targets help the student more than hard labels? What does the temperature actually change?

Soft targets help because they encode relative similarities between classes, which a one-hot label cannot. A hard label says only that the answer is class A, while the teacher's distribution might assign 0.7 to A, 0.2 to a similar class B, and 0.001 to an unrelated class C. This gives the student richer gradient signal and a regularizing effect, since it learns the structure of the output space rather than memorizing single correct answers. Temperature T divides the logits before the softmax. At T=1 the distribution is usually peaked on the top class, so the small probabilities of wrong classes are nearly invisible. Raising T to values such as 3 or 5 flattens the distribution and magnifies those secondary probabilities. Hinton and colleagues often multiply the distillation loss by T squared so that gradient magnitudes stay comparable as T changes.
Are there distillation methods that go beyond matching output probabilities, and how do they differ?

Yes, several approaches transfer more than final outputs. Feature-based methods, such as FitNets, add a loss that pushes intermediate hidden representations of the student toward those of the teacher, often through a learned projection layer when the dimensions differ. Attention transfer asks the student to reproduce the teacher's attention maps. Relation-based methods go further and match the pairwise relationships between examples in a batch, such as the similarity structure among embeddings, rather than the individual activations. Self-distillation uses a model as its own teacher, for instance by training a deeper network's later layers to mimic its earlier ones or by using an earlier checkpoint. The main trade-off is that intermediate-feature methods can give stronger guidance but require architectural alignment and extra tuning, while output-only distillation is simpler, more general, and works even when the teacher's internals are inaccessible.
How does a mixture of experts model work?

A mixture of experts (MoE) model splits a large network into several specialized subnetworks called experts, each usually a feed-forward block. A small learned component called a gating network, or router, looks at each input and produces a score for every expert. In the common sparse variant, only the top-k experts with the highest scores (often k=1 or 2) are activated for that input, and their outputs are combined using the gate weights. Because only a fraction of the parameters run for any given token, the model can have a very large total parameter count while keeping the compute per token close to that of a much smaller dense model. Training encourages the router to send different kinds of inputs to different experts, which gives the experts room to specialize.
What's the difference between sparse and dense mixture of experts?

In a dense mixture of experts, the gating network assigns weights to all experts and every expert processes every input, with the outputs blended by those weights. This gives smooth, fully differentiable behavior but offers no compute savings, since each expert always runs. A sparse mixture of experts instead keeps only the top-k experts per input, zeroing out the rest. Compute scales with k rather than the total number of experts, so models can grow to hundreds of billions of parameters at manageable cost. The tradeoff is added complexity: sparse routing creates discrete choices that are harder to optimize, and it can cause uneven load, where a few experts receive most tokens. Sparse designs therefore usually add auxiliary load-balancing losses or capacity limits per expert.
How do load-balancing losses work in those sparse models?

A common approach adds an auxiliary loss term to the training objective that penalizes uneven routing. In the Switch Transformer formulation, for each expert i the method computes f_i, the fraction of tokens dispatched to that expert, and P_i, the average router probability assigned to it across a batch. The auxiliary loss is N times the sum of f_i multiplied by P_i, where N is the number of experts, and it is minimized when tokens and probabilities are spread uniformly. Because f_i itself is not differentiable, gradients flow through P_i. Other systems use capacity factors, which cap how many tokens each expert can accept per batch; overflow tokens are skipped or passed through a residual connection. Some newer methods avoid auxiliary losses altogether by adjusting per-expert routing biases dynamically based on recent load.
Why do experts often end up specializing in things like punctuation or syntax rather than topics?

Analyses of trained MoE language models, including work on Mixtral and Switch Transformer, often find that routing is strongly tied to token-level features rather than high-level topics. The router is a linear function of the token's hidden representation, so it tends to group tokens by surface properties such as punctuation, whitespace, casing, or part of speech. Routing decisions are made independently at each layer and each token, and the router sees only local representations, so it has little incentive to coordinate around semantic domains. Load-balancing losses also push toward splitting tokens by frequent, easily separable patterns. As a result, expert specialization is often syntactic or lexical, and topic-level specialization is weaker and less consistent across layers than early hopes suggested.
How does paged attention work in vLLM?

Paged attention in vLLM stores the key-value (KV) cache in fixed-size blocks rather than one contiguous tensor per sequence. Each block holds the keys and values for a set number of tokens, typically 16 by default. A block table maps each sequence's logical token positions to physical block IDs, much like a page table in an operating system maps virtual pages to physical frames. During the attention computation, a custom CUDA kernel reads the keys and values by following this block table, so the blocks for one sequence do not need to be adjacent in GPU memory. Blocks are allocated on demand as a sequence grows and returned to a free pool when a request finishes or is preempted. This removes most of the memory fragmentation and over-reservation that occurred when systems pre-allocated the maximum sequence length for every request.
What happens when the block pool runs out of free blocks?

When no free physical blocks remain, the scheduler must free memory before it can admit or continue requests. vLLM supports two preemption strategies. The default for most cases is recomputation: the scheduler evicts a running sequence, discards its KV cache blocks, and later re-runs the prefill over its prompt plus the tokens generated so far. The other strategy is swapping, where the evicted blocks are copied to CPU memory and copied back when the sequence resumes. Recomputation avoids the PCIe transfer cost and is often faster for shorter sequences, while swapping can be better when recomputing is expensive. Preemption victims are usually chosen from the most recently admitted requests, so that older requests make steady progress.
How does block sharing work when several requests use the same prompt prefix?

Because blocks are indirected through a block table, two sequences can point to the same physical block. vLLM uses reference counting on each block. When requests share a prefix, such as a common system prompt or the parallel samples generated for one prompt, their block tables reference the same KV blocks for those tokens, and the reference count is incremented. Sharing is copy-on-write: when one sequence must write a new token into a block that is still shared, vLLM allocates a fresh block, copies the contents, and updates only that sequence's block table. Automatic prefix caching extends this idea by hashing full blocks by their token content, so a later request with the same prefix can reuse cached blocks even after the original request has finished. This reduces both memory use and prefill computation.
What is a KV cache in the context of transformer language models?

A KV cache stores the key and value tensors computed for each token in the attention layers of a transformer. During autoregressive generation, the model produces one token at a time, and each new token's attention needs the keys and values of all previous tokens. Without caching, those tensors would be recomputed from scratch at every step, which wastes computation. With the cache, the model computes the key and value vectors only for the newest token, appends them to the stored tensors, and runs attention over the full cached sequence. This trades memory for speed: the cache grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, number of layers, and number of attention heads, and it is typically kept in GPU memory during inference.
Why does the cache need to store keys and values but not queries?

Attention computes, for each position, a weighted sum over all earlier positions, where the weights come from comparing a query with every key. The query only matters for the token currently being generated, so once that token has been processed, its query is never needed again. Keys and values, however, are reused by every future token, since each later query must be compared against all prior keys and the output mixes all prior values. Storing queries would therefore add memory without enabling any reuse. In practice, the cache holds two tensors per layer, one for keys and one for values, each shaped by sequence length and head dimension, and only the newest row is written at each decoding step.
How much memory does a KV cache actually take for a large model?

A useful estimate is 2 times the number of layers, times the number of KV heads, times the head dimension, times the sequence length, times the batch size, times bytes per element. The factor of 2 accounts for keys and values. For example, a model with 32 layers, 32 KV heads, a head dimension of 128, and fp16 values (2 bytes) needs about 0.5 MB per token, so a single 4096-token sequence uses roughly 2 GB. Batching multiple requests multiplies this. Grouped-query attention reduces the number of KV heads, often by a factor of 4 to 8, which shrinks the cache proportionally. Quantizing the cache to 8-bit or lower precision is another common way to cut memory use.
What techniques do systems use to manage KV cache memory efficiently?

Several approaches address fragmentation and waste. PagedAttention, used in vLLM, divides the cache into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, similar to virtual memory paging, so sequences do not need one large contiguous region. Prefix caching lets requests that share a common prompt reuse the same stored blocks instead of recomputing them. Eviction and compression methods drop or merge less important entries, for example keeping recent tokens and a few high-attention tokens. Offloading moves older cache blocks to CPU memory or disk when GPU memory is scarce. Continuous batching then fills the freed space with new requests, which raises overall throughput while keeping latency manageable.
What is speculative decoding and why is it used for large language models?

Speculative decoding is a technique for speeding up autoregressive text generation without changing the output distribution. Standard decoding produces one token per forward pass of the large target model, and each pass is often limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic, so the hardware sits underutilized. The method uses a smaller, faster draft model to propose several tokens ahead. The large target model then checks all of those proposed tokens in a single parallel forward pass. Tokens that match what the target model would have sampled are accepted, and at the first mismatch the target's own token is used instead. Because each verification step can yield multiple accepted tokens, latency drops while the final text remains statistically identical to what the target model alone would produce.
How does the verification step decide which draft tokens to accept?

Verification uses a modified rejection sampling scheme. For each drafted token x, let p be the target model's probability for x and q be the draft model's probability for x. The token is accepted with probability min(1, p/q). If it is rejected, a replacement token is sampled from the normalized residual distribution max(0, p - q), which is the part of the target distribution the draft did not cover. This correction guarantees that the accepted output follows the target distribution exactly. With greedy decoding, the rule simplifies: a draft token is accepted only if it equals the target model's argmax at that position. Processing proceeds left to right, and once one token is rejected, the remaining drafted tokens are discarded.
What factors determine how much speedup you actually get from this approach?

The main factors are the acceptance rate, the relative cost of the draft model, and the number of tokens drafted per step. The acceptance rate depends on how closely the draft model's distribution matches the target's, and it is often higher for easy or predictable text such as code boilerplate.
